The BBC previously tried unsuccessfully to serve subpoenas in person to Trump's family members before asking a judge for permission to use certified mail.
Trump's $10 billion defamation lawsuit claims the BBC deceptively edited his January 6, 2021, speech to interfere with the 2024 presidential election.
The BBC has apologized to Trump for the misleading edit in its documentary, but denies defaming him.
U.S. District Judge Jeffrey Kuntz inherited the case and did not immediately rule on the subpoena dispute.

title: Holding election in wartime would risk destroying Ukraine, says Zelenskyy
author: Dan Sabbagh
content:
Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said holding elections in Ukraine during wartime would risk splitting the country at a time when Russia is amassing ballistic missiles and considering whether to mobilise an extra 300,000 soldiers.
The Ukrainian president, responding for the first time to a demand made by the sacked former defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov, sharply criticised an idea that he said was impractical given Russia appeared to have no interest in a ceasefire.
“I believe that if we want to destroy the country, then during such a war we can move in the selection of elections,” Zelenskyy said in a briefing to selected journalists that was held on Saturday, but details of which were reported on Sunday.
“I believe that during such a war, elections in general are big risks. Elections right now are a tsunami for the state that will split Ukraine,” he said, adding that his plan was to end the war and preserve Ukraine as an independent state.
Elections have been suspended in Ukraine since martial law was imposed at the start of the full-scale invasion by Russia. Zelenskyy’s five-year term ended in May 2024 but there had until recently been little desire in Ukraine to hold a contest while the war continued.
That shifted when Fedorov, a popular minister who had been dismissed by Zelenskyy a month earlier, called for a fresh contest. It was the most open challenge to Zelenskyy’s authority from inside Ukraine since the start of the Russian invasion.
Zelenskyy said, according to a transcript from the briefing, that if Ukraine’s allies were to establish “specific conditions” under which elections could be safely, legitimately and democratically held in Ukraine, he would support them.
It would require “the participation of the military, in frontline territories, abroad, where millions of our citizens have gone, fleeing the war” and a poll would have to take place safely “without strikes and shelling”, he said.
Fedorov, he said, had moved from his post because had had overreached, trying to cover functions belonging to the military. He had been offered four alternative jobs in the government but declined all four, the president added. “I really had and still have a very positive attitude toward Mykhailo,” Zelenskyy said. “We have been through a lot together. But I believe that he himself goes, or is pushed, into the wrong things.”
Russia had a stockpile of 600-630 high-speed ballistic missiles, its most potent type of weapon, and was trying to build a little more than 100 more a month in the run-up to winter, Zelenskyy said. Its maximum production capacity was 1,300 a year, he added.
Ballistic missiles have been used to bomb Ukrainian infrastructure and warehouses and to attack the capital, causing increased civilian casualties. There is a shortage of US-made Patriot interceptors, the only weapon that can effectively counter them.
“I wanted to secure 300 Patriot missiles for the winter package. The request from our air force is 360,” Zelenskyy said. He acknowledged this was difficult given that only about 600 of the most capable PAC-3 interceptor missiles were made a year. He said he had reached an agreement with France on at least one SAMP/T air-defence system this year, and with Germany on the supply of about 600 PAC-2 and PAC-3 interceptors in 2027--28.
after newsletter promotion
The US could help by supplying “some small percentage” of its stockpiles – about 5% to 10%, he added. Ukraine was willing to pay and it would mean the country “could get through the winter”, he said, calling on the US to make what would be “a very significant difference both in protecting lives and diplomatically”.
Following a conversation with Zelenskyy on Saturday, the French president, Emmanuel Macron, said he had agreed to strengthen French support for Ukraine, including through the delivery of interceptor missiles, without giving further details.
Ukraine’s allies in the so-called coalition of the willing – an initiative led by France and Britain – will meet on Monday to look at how to ramp up pressure on Moscow to halt its invasion.
Russia is seeking to build up forces for a renewed effort to capture the rest of the eastern Donetsk province it does not control by the end of the year, though Zelenskyy said he was confident Moscow would fail to capture the area, comprising principally the cities of Kramatorsk and Sloviansk.
The president said he believed Russia would try to conscript a further 300,000 soldiers after the Russian parliamentary elections in September. It would be a “peripheral mobilisation” conducted away from Moscow, St Petersburg and other main cities in an effort to regain momentum in the almost deadlocked frontline, he said.
summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has stated that holding elections during wartime would risk splitting the country and destroying the state amid ongoing Russian aggression. Responding to calls for a fresh election from sacked former minister Mykhailo Fedorov, Zelenskyy maintained that a vote is impractical while Russia continues its attacks and lacks interest in a ceasefire. He noted, however, that he would support elections if allies established safe and democratic conditions for all citizens, including the military and refugees abroad. Zelenskyy also warned that Russia is stockpiling ballistic missiles and planning a mobilization of 300,000 additional soldiers.
key_points: Zelenskyy warned that holding wartime elections would act as a tsunami that could split Ukraine.
Elections have been suspended under martial law since the full-scale Russian invasion began.
Former defense minister Mykhailo Fedorov challenged Zelenskyy's authority by calling for a fresh election.
Zelenskyy stated he would support elections only if allies guarantee safe and democratic conditions for voters, soldiers, and refugees.
Ukraine is seeking additional air defense interceptors from allies, including the US, France, and Germany, to counter Russian ballistic missile attacks.

title: Zelenskyy says wartime elections could ‘destroy’ Ukraine
author: Al Jazeera Staff
content:
![Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy](https://www.aljazeera.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/reuters_6a8acc62-1787481186.jpg?resize=770%2C513&quality=80)
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has rejected his ex-defence chief’s calls for a wartime election, calling the prospect a “huge risk” amid the more than four-year war with Russia.
Ukrainian law bans elections during wartime, a measure that had gone unchallenged until former Defence Minister Mykhailo Fedorov made the first public demand for a vote earlier this week.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Russia says ready for ‘new ideas’ on Ukraine war that match Putin’s goals
- list 2 of 4Russian expert warns of impending social crisis as Ukraine death toll rises
- list 3 of 4Russian drone attack on busy shopping centre kills 15 in Ukraine
- list 4 of 4Russia, Ukraine trade attacks as Putin warns of ‘far more destructive’ hits
Zelenskyy rejected the call during a wide-ranging briefing with reporters on Saturday.
“I believe that in a war like this, elections as such are a huge risk. Elections right now are a tsunami for the country that will split Ukraine,” the president said in comments published on Sunday.
“If we want to destroy the country, then we can move in the direction of elections during these times of war,” he added.
The 35-year-old Fedorov – a popular figure in Ukraine – held his post for just six months until Zelenskyy fired him in July, prompting protests across the country.
On Tuesday, he posted an explosive nine-minute video on YouTube claiming that Ukraine’s democracy “cannot be held hostage by Russia”.
“Can Russia actually be entitled to define when Ukrainians can elect their authorities next time? I’m sure it’s not,” he said, adding that Kyiv faces a “systemic crisis of governance”.
Experts have told Al Jazeera, however, that any wartime election would be practically impossible amid logistical and safety challenges, a reality that most Ukrainians agree with.
Kyiv tackles missile launchers, Starlink
Zelenskyy’s domestic political crisis is playing out as his government seeks more ways to curtail Moscow’s deadly air strikes.
Overnight Russian strikes in the eastern Donetsk region killed two people and wounded two others on Sunday, Ukraine’s emergency services said on Telegram. At least 141 private homes sustained damage in the attack.
Another eight people, including a child, were wounded in a drone attack on the northeastern city of Kharkiv that burned at least two residential buildings, the service said.
Meanwhile in the Odesa region, a Russian drone hit a passenger train travelling from Zhytomyr to Odesa, the Kyiv Independent reported, citing Ukrainian Railways CEO Oleksandr Pertsovskyi. No casualties were reported.
Amid the attacks, Zelenskyy said on Saturday that Ukraine is especially focused on hitting Russian ballistic launchers as Moscow ramps up its use of missiles – which effectively can only be destroyed by US-designed Patriot systems.
Ukraine has received just 264 Patriot missiles in 2026, down from 364 in 2025 and 675 in 2023, he said.
“When our antiballistic missiles are minimised – here is another tactic … hunting their nearby locations from which ballistic missiles are launched,” Zelenskyy said.
Ukraine is seeking to produce Patriot missiles domestically after receiving political blessing from United States President Donald Trump.
The Ukrainian president also said Moscow and Kyiv are building their own versions of Starlink, the satellite system used for battlefield communications that is controlled by US tech billionaire Elon Musk.
Russia’s alternative, developed “together with the Chinese”, is expected to be operational by December, Zelenskyy said.
He added that Ukraine would not “just sit and wait for Russia and China” and was “implementing a similar project with a European country”.
![FILE PHOTO: A serviceman of the 20th Separate K-2 Unmanned Systems Brigade of the Unmanned Systems Forces prepares to launch a FP-2 middle strike drone towards Russian troops, amid Russia's attack on Ukraine, in Kharkiv region, Ukraine August 17, 2026. REUTERS/Sofiia Gatilova/File Photo](https://www.aljazeera.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/2026-08-22T165704Z_1554331863_RC2J0NAJ0S67_RTRMADP_3_UKRAINE-CRISIS-RUSSIA-DRONES-1787483240.jpg?w=770&resize=770%2C539&quality=80)
Funding gap
Ukraine’s wartime efforts may be hampered by a $27bn defence funding gap this year, Zelenskyy said, following defence spending that was higher than expected in the first half of 2026.
Ukraine needs at least $8bn for “a normal start” to 2027, he said, in addition to about $20bn more for other spending such as military salaries and payments to families of the dead.
Ukraine has reached an agreement with France for at least one SAMP/T air defence system this year, Zelenskyy said, and with Germany on the supply of about 600 PAC-2 and PAC-3 interceptors through 2028.
Norway said on Sunday it would give 85 billion crowns ($9.2bn) to Kyiv for the 2027 fiscal year, in line with what it provided in 2026.
summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has rejected calls from his former defence chief to hold wartime elections, warning that a vote would pose a massive risk and split the country. Meanwhile, continuing Russian air strikes have caused casualties and infrastructure damage across multiple regions in Ukraine. Amid a $27bn defence funding gap for the year, Ukraine is focusing on domestic missile production, targeting Russian launch sites, and securing international air defense support.
key_points: Ukrainian law bans wartime elections, but former Defence Minister Mykhailo Fedorov publicly demanded a vote, citing a governance crisis.
President Zelenskyy rejected the election demand, stating that holding a vote during the war could destroy and split the country.
Recent Russian drone and missile attacks across Ukraine have killed civilians and damaged residential buildings and infrastructure.
Ukraine faces a $27bn defence funding gap this year and is working to secure military aid, air defence systems, and domestic missile production.
Zelenskyy announced that both Russia and Ukraine are developing their own versions of satellite communication systems similar to Starlink.

title: Ukraine war latest: Zelensky claims Putin drafting 300,000 troops to seize territory
author: Alisha Rahaman Sarkar; Sam Rkaina; Rebecca Whittaker
content:
Ukraine’s president Volodymyr Zelensky has warned that Vladimir Putin intends to draft 300,000 new troops to join the war from next month in a bid to seize territory.
Zelensky said that the Russian leader would start the drive after elections in September, for Moscow’s key goal of capturing the rest of Ukraine's eastern Donetsk region.
In other comments on Sunday, the Ukrainian leader claimed that holding a wartime election would “destroy” the country by splitting its citizens.
He was responding to calls from his former Defence Minister Mykhailo Fedorov for the country to go to the polls despite the ongoing conflict with Russia.
Meanwhile, Putin has pulled Russia’s ambassador from London, accusing Britain of taking the “path of confrontation”, as relations between the two countries continue to deteriorate.
Andrey Kelin, who served as the Russian ambassador to the UK for over seven years, vacated his post last month.
UK prime minister Andy Burnham said the country is continuing to “support Ukraine 100 per cent” after Moscow threatened consequences for the reported use of British drones for strikes deep into Russia.
Ukraine braces for new wave of energy strikes
Ukraine is facing another difficult winter of Russian strikes on its energy grid, President Zelensky has warned, a prospect that had prompted Kyiv's air force to ask for 360 missile interceptors for the season.
He also said he had reached an agreement with France on at least one SAMP/T air-defence system this year, and with Germany on the supply of about 600 PAC-2 and PAC-3 interceptors through 2028.
Ukraine's war effort is further complicated by a $27 billion defence funding gap this year, Zelensky added, a result of higher-than-expected spending in the first half of the year.
At least $8 billion is needed for "a normal start" to 2027, plus about $20 billion more for military salaries, payments to families of the dead, as well as other financing, the president said.
Minister pays tribute to ‘courage’ of Ukrainians ahead of independence day event
A Scottish Government minister has paid tribute to the “extraordinary courage, determination and resilience” of the people of Ukraine, ahead of the country’s independence day on Monday.
Minister for Europe and external affairs Stephen Gethin made the comments ahead of an appearance at an Association of Ukrainians in Great Britain event in Glasgow on Sunday, where he will address Ukrainians and supporters.
He is expected to pay tribute to the resilience of the Ukrainian people, recognising their contribution to communities across Scotland, and reiterating the Scottish Government’s unwavering support for Ukraine.
Speaking ahead of the event, Mr Gethin said: “As Ukraine continues to defend its freedom, and the freedoms of everyone in democratic Europe, its people continue to demonstrate extraordinary courage, determination and resilience.
“Their strength in the face of Russia’s aggression, violence and oppression remains an inspiration to people around the world.”
Ukraine marks Day of the National Flag
![](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/08/23/15/2026-08-23T100039Z_1688733427_RC274NAZYAZ2_RTRMADP_3_UKRAINE-CRISIS-FLAG-DAY.JPG)
![](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/08/23/15/2026-08-23T102341Z_342982441_RC274NAXWV1N_RTRMADP_3_UKRAINE-CRISIS-FLAG-DAY.JPG)
Ukraine elections now would be 'tsunami for the state'
Zelensky's approval rating has remained generally stable at about 60%, but pollsters have said that while Ukrainians want fresh faces in politics, many have little appetite for voting now.
An August 5 poll by the Kyiv International Institute of Sociology found that 57% of Ukrainians want elections only after fighting ends.
Echoing his previous comments on the matter, Zelensky said a wartime election might be possible if Kyiv's partners could guarantee security, but that no one has proposed such a plan.
“Elections right now are a tsunami for the state, which will split Ukraine,” he said.
“That's why my strategy is to steer the country toward an ending of the war and to preserve an independent and sovereign state.”
Putin says Ukrainian strikes cause losses but won't turn tide of war
Wartime election would 'destroy' Ukraine, Zelensky says
Holding a wartime election in Ukraine while active fighting with Russia continues would “destroy” the country by splitting Ukrainians, President Volodymyr Zelensky said.
His comments, released to reporters on Sunday, were Zelensky's first on the subject since ousted former Defence Minister Mykhailo Fedorov called for a wartime poll in an address last week.
Fedorov's surprise dismissal last month sparked widespread protests, but supporters calling for his reinstatement later baulked at his call for an election - the first such demand by a major Ukrainian political figure since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022.
“I believe that if we want to destroy the country, then we can move towards elections during this kind of war,” Zelensky said.
![Mykhailo Fedorov](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/08/23/12/2026-08-19T113929Z_481899326_RC2W4MA9SE7O_RTRMADP_3_UKRAINE-CRISIS-FEDOROV.JPG)
Ukraine facing shortage of Patriot interceptors
Russia is bolstering its battlefield offensive with an escalating air war on Ukrainian cities made worse by a critical shortage of U.S.-designed Patriot interceptors.
Zelensky said the 264 interceptors Ukraine is expecting to have received in 2026 represent a significant drop from 2025, when Ukraine received 364, and 2023, when it received 675.
He added that Russia was aiming to develop a capacity to produce up to 1,300 ballistic missiles per year.
Over the summer, Ukraine has escalated a campaign of drone strikes targeting Russian economic infrastructure, including oil refineries and online retailers' warehouses, seeking to destroy infrastructure it says is central to Russia's war effort.
Russian President Vladimir Putin said in comments on Saturday that Kyiv had opened "Pandora's box" by striking economic targets, saying Russia would hit back at Ukraine's "most sensitive economic sectors".
![](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/08/23/11/2026-08-23T095230Z_1128688101_RC274NA1775D_RTRMADP_3_UKRAINE-CRISIS-FLAG-DAY.JPG)
Norway to give over $9 billion to Ukraine in 2027
Norway plans to give another 85 billion Norwegian crowns ($9.2 billion) in financial support to Ukraine in the 2027 fiscal year, in line with the amount given in 2026, the Nordic country's government said in a statement on Sunday.
Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Stoere and leaders from across the Nordic and Baltic region are visiting Kyiv on Sunday in a show of support for Ukraine in the war with Russia.
Norway’s donation will be for both military and humanitarian spending, Stoere was quoted as saying in the text of a speech released by the government in Oslo.
“Supporting and rebuilding Ukraine is not assistance alone. It is an investment in Europe's own security,” Stoere said.
Putin will draft 300,000 new troops after September elections, Zelensky says
Ukraine believes Russia is planning to mobilise an additional 300,000 troops for its war effort after parliamentary elections in September, President Volodymyr Zelensky said.
In comments to reporters released on Sunday, Zelensky added that Russia could draft hundreds of thousands more in 2027 for its key goal of capturing the rest of Ukraine's eastern Donetsk region.
Russian online retailer Ozon warehouse in Orenburg region hit in drone attack
Two industrial facilities were hit by drone debris, including a warehouse owned by Ozon, a major Russian online retailer.
The governor of Russia's Orenburg region Yevgeny Solntsev said that the Russian defence ministry had repelled six drones over the region, adding that no one had been injured. He did not name the second damaged facility.
Russia's defence ministry said it downed 328 Ukrainian drones overnight.
Ozon, Russia's second-largest online retailer, said in a statement on Telegram that the company had evacuated more than 300 people and that work at its Orenburg region logistics centre had been halted.
summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky warned that Russia plans to draft 300,000 new troops following September elections to capture the eastern Donetsk region. Zelensky also stated that holding a wartime election would split and destroy the country, responding to recent calls for a vote amidst the ongoing conflict. Meanwhile, Ukraine faces a challenging winter energy outlook, a multibillion-dollar defense funding gap, and critical shortages of missile interceptors while securing continued international support.
key_points: President Zelensky claims Vladimir Putin intends to draft 300,000 new troops after September elections to capture the rest of the Donetsk region.
Zelensky stated that holding a wartime election would destroy Ukraine by splitting its citizens.
Ukraine is facing a $27 billion defense funding gap this year and anticipates a difficult winter of Russian strikes on its energy grid.
Norway announced plans to provide $9.2 billion in financial support to Ukraine for the 2027 fiscal year.
Russia pulled its ambassador from London as diplomatic relations between Moscow and the UK continue to deteriorate.

title: Zelensky should be asked what he knew about government corruption, ex-minister Mykhailo Fedorov tells BBC
author: Dan Johnson
content:
Fedorov asked about Ukraine government corruption claims
- Published
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky should be asked questions about corruption in his government, his sacked defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov has told the BBC.
Fedorov, a popular minister who modernised the military and pioneered drone warfare, was fired last month after reportedly falling out with the head of Ukraine's armed forces.
He told the BBC a money laundering investigation announced last week meant Zelensky should be asked about his awareness of potential corruption in his inner circle.
But he said he had not himself seen the president engage in any corrupt activity.
"In all the time that I worked with him, not a single time have I received from him any task or assignment that would go against law or my sense of integrity", Federov said.
The former minister also repeated his appeal for elections to be held in Ukraine, days after releasing a video where he called for a wartime vote.
"Democracy should not be the hostage of Putin", he said - but stopped short of declaring his own political ambitions.
There were angry protests over Fedorov's sacking but his support dwindled and demonstrations ended on Wednesday, after his replacement was confirmed. His call for a vote has been widely rejected.
Asked whether he missed his old job, the 35-year-old replied "No", citing the relentless stress of managing Ukraine's war with Russia while transforming its defence ministry.
Ukraine has been under martial law since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022, meaning elections are suspended. Zelensky's five-year presidential term ended in May 2024.
But Fedorov said it was his "moral right" to start the conversation about elections.
"We should not be afraid of discussing it. That's what democracy is all about. If I cannot share my ideas and be open about them with my own society, then what are we fighting for?"
If elections were never held, he said, "then we are no longer a democracy".
![A man dressed in a white T-shirt and brown collared shirt in front of a black background sits talking to someone with their back to the camera.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2560/cpsprodpb/f1da/live/9dcc87a0-9ecc-11f1-a6c1-71ec82f18bdc.jpg)
Federov has called for elections and declined to answer if he backs Zelensky
In his earlier video statement Fedorov had argued that "people cannot endlessly live in a state where they do not understand why certain decisions are made".
He shied away from criticising the president directly and declined to answer whether he backs Zelensky to win any election.
Zelensky said he believed wartime elections would currently be too dangerous for Ukraine in remarks released on Sunday.
"I believe that in a war like this, elections as such are a huge risk," he said. "Elections right now are a tsunami for the country that will split Ukraine."
Experts have cited a number of obstacles to holding such a vote, including how soldiers, millions of Ukrainian refugees and people from occupied territories would vote, as well as disinformation threats from Russia.
Fedorov's video highlighting political corruption last week came the day before a money laundering investigation was announced into lawmakers and bankers.
Ukraine's anti-corruption bureau said it had uncovered a scheme to misappropriate more than $3m (Â£2.2m) in Ukrainian currency to pay bail for a former energy minister accused of money laundering.
A senior official in Zelensky's office, alleged to be involved, was sacked.
![A man in a black suit and shirt sits between other people at a desk with countries' flags in the background and a table sign at the front that reads Ukraine next to a Ukrainian flag.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/db65/live/ff7bda70-9ea7-11f1-a291-b542ee92de7c.jpg)
Mikhailo Fedorov at a meeting of the Ukraine Defence Contact Group in Belgium in February
Fedorov said there were questions about the president's awareness of potential corruption in his inner circle.
"Let him answer this question... I believe that he's ready for such questions. It's his responsibility to tell us all whether he was aware of all that or not... I don't want to make any assumptions."
A spokesperson for the president had earlier told BBC News: "Since the former minister was part of every government since 2019, it's strange that he phrases it as though these were somehow different governments without him. As everyone remembers, we didn't hear any strong statements from him back then."
Fedorov claimed he had rooted out elements of corruption from defence procurement but warned it was still affecting Ukraine's frontline capacity.
The former minister said he'd had no contact with the president for "a couple of weeks", and had no evidence the president was personally corrupt.
"In all the time that I worked with him, not a single time have I received from him any task or assignment that would go against law or my sense of integrity. So that's my personal experience with him."
Ukraine's sacked defence minister defends election calls in BBC interview
As defence minister and previously digital transformation minister, Fedorov is credited with innovating to replace soldiers with an "army of drones", saving lives on the battlefield and enabling long-range Ukrainian strikes on Russian military targets, oil refineries and distribution warehouses - thousands of kilometres over the border.
He said he would continue to promote new ways to fight the war and confirmed a visit to the United States in the coming weeks, where he hopes to meet Elon Musk.
The billionaire businessman's Starlink satellite communications system has been key in Ukraine's success. Fedorov aims to convince Musk to extend the technology into Russian airspace to assist Ukrainian strikes, without the Kremlin benefiting from access.
"The best tech companies in the world are supporting us and they will be investing in our victory, in ending this war. And we need to stay in touch with them regardless of my position. I have a previous successful track record of working with them and I need to stay in touch with them for my country," he said.
![President Volodymyr Zelensky standing smiling with his hand in a hi-five next to another politician also dressed in black in front of a blue background with the Nato symbol and the Ukrainian flag.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2560/cpsprodpb/20ae/live/d9b3ce50-9ea8-11f1-a291-b542ee92de7c.jpg)
President Zelensky with Fedorov during a Nato meeting in June
Fedorov criticised bureaucracy in the UK and other countries supporting Ukraine for delays in supplying weapons.
The UK is a longstanding supporter of Ukraine, spending Â£16bn supplying weapons since the war began. It was confirmed last week that British-made drones have been used to attack Russian targets.
Fedorov said he was grateful for British support but blamed "bureaucracy and red tape" for delays in receiving promised equipment.
"Governments are lagging behind the realities on the ground. It's not only the issue for UK, but for other countries as well that announce some assistance and we are not getting it until the end of the year."
Fedorov urged direct funding of the latest Ukrainian drone production, in place of outdated skills and equipment from other nations: "We don't need repairs of tanks when we no longer use tanks."
He said timely deliveries would help save not just Ukrainian lives.
"Unfortunately, our losses, our blood, our military experience is beneficial to all of you guys. You can get this experience for all the assistance that you give us."
Fedorov denied having immediate political ambitions but didn't rule out a future run for president.
"It will all depend on how soon we'll be able to relaunch this democratic election process, [...] how much energy I would have, whether I will preserve my team, whether I will be able to respond to the question myself, whether I can handle this position of the president or not.
"What's more important, is whether people will tell me, yeah, we can trust you handling that position."
Correction 23 August: This article originally said Mykhailo Fedorov's video highlighting political corruption was released the same day a money laundering investigation was announced into lawmakers and bankers. It has been corrected to reflect that the video was released the day before the announcement.
summary: Recently sacked Ukrainian defense minister Mykhailo Fedorov told the BBC that President Volodymyr Zelensky should face questions regarding potential corruption within his inner circle following a recent money laundering investigation. Fedorov also defended his recent calls for wartime elections to be held in Ukraine despite martial law and widespread rejection of the idea. However, Fedorov stated he has not personally witnessed Zelensky engage in any corrupt activity and noted he has no immediate political ambitions.
key_points: Mykhailo Fedorov stated that President Zelensky should answer questions regarding awareness of corruption within his inner circle following a money laundering investigation.
Fedorov stated he never personally received any unlawful tasks or assignments from Zelensky during their time working together.
Fedorov defended his recent public calls for wartime elections to be held in Ukraine, arguing that democracy must not be a hostage of war.
President Zelensky and critics have rejected immediate wartime elections, citing severe security risks and logistical obstacles.

title: Putin to draft 300,000 new troops in September, says Zelensky
author: Emily Smith
content:
![Vladimir Putin among Russian troops](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/world-news/2026/08/23/TELEMMGLPICT000483400388_17874802095711_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqpVlberWd9EgFPZtcLiMQf0Rf_Wk3V23H2268P_XkPxc.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![Vladimir Putin among Russian troops](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/world-news/2026/08/23/TELEMMGLPICT000483400388_17874802095711_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqpVlberWd9EgFPZtcLiMQf0Rf_Wk3V23H2268P_XkPxc.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
Vladimir Putin will draft 300,000 new troops after Russia’s elections in September, Volodymyr Zelensky has claimed.
The Ukrainian president said Moscow could draft thousands more in 2027 to capture the rest of Ukraine’s Donetsk region.
Donetsk is one of the four Ukrainian regions, alongside Luhansk, Kherson and Zaporizhzhia, that Putin claimed to have annexed in 2022 despite only occupying part of each territory.
Moscow holds at least 80 per cent of Donetsk, and capturing the remainder has become one of the Kremlin’s central objectives.
The new troops may aid Moscow in capturing the remaining Ukrainian-held territory, including the Fortress Belt, which Russia has been pushing towards for months.
Moscow has also begun conducting exercises to test its readiness for a fresh military mobilisation, including a planning exercise in Kaliningrad last month to prepare for calling up residents.
Western intelligence officials told the The Wall Street Journal that the exercises tested how Russia would house, feed and arm new recruits as Russia struggles to replenish its forces through voluntary recruitment.
Mr Zelensky has also dismissed suggestions from his ousted defence minister to call for an election.
Mykhailo Fedorov, who was dismissed from his post last month, demanded an election, declaring in a video posted on YouTube: “Democracy cannot be held hostage by Russia.
“We must find a legal, safe and realistic mechanism that will allow Ukraine to restore a full democratic process, even amidst a prolonged war.”
![Mykhailo Fedorov](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/world-news/2026/08/23/TELEMMGLPICT000498848285_17874789443820_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqpVlberWd9EgFPZtcLiMQf0Rf_Wk3V23H2268P_XkPxc.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
However, Mr Zelensky said wartime elections would be too dangerous for Ukraine.
During his first press briefing in months, he said: “I believe that in a war like this, elections as such are a huge risk. Elections right now are a tsunami for the country that will split Ukraine.”
Ukraine has suspended elections under martial law, a measure still widely supported by the population as the country focuses on fighting off Russian forces.
“If we want to destroy the country, then we can move in the direction of elections during these times of war,” Mr Zelensky added in remarks that were made public on Sunday.
![Volodymyr Zelensky](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/world-news/2026/08/23/TELEMMGLPICT000499290440_17874931495550_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqpVlberWd9EgFPZtcLiMQf0Rf_Wk3V23H2268P_XkPxc.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
Meanwhile, Ukraine has made Russia’s second-largest online retailer the target of its long-range drone strikes.
After targeting several warehouses belonging to Wildberries, Russia’s answer to Amazon, Kyiv has struck two Ozon facilities in the southern regions of Samara and Orenburg.
Ozon is responsible for around 30 per cent of Russia’s e-commerce market.
Kyiv’s attacks on retailer warhouses are intended to put economic pressure on Moscow and “bring the war home” to ordinary Russians.
The first attack came on a warehouse in Samara on Saturday, followed by a second in Orenburg overnight on Sunday.
Video footage on social media showed flames and smoke billowing from the warehouses, while firefighters worked to tackle the blaze.
Orenburg is close to the Kazakhstan border, around 620 miles from the Russia-Ukraine border, demonstrating Ukraine’s increasing long-range capability.
Ozon said in a statement on Telegram that the company had evacuated more than 300 people and had halted work at its Orenburg region logistics centre.
The strikes came just one day after Ukraine targeted the first warehouse belonging to Ozon in Samara on Friday. A major fire tore through the facility, and more than 500 staff were evacuated.
In a statement on Telegram, Ozon said that work at its Samara region logistics centre in the town of Chapayevsk had been halted after the strike, which it said caused injuries.
Ukraine has also insisted Wildberries was being used as a key supply chain for the Russian military.
![A Wildberries employee at the site of a Ukrainian strike](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/world-news/2026/08/23/TELEMMGLPICT000498566562_17874790232460_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqpVlberWd9EgFPZtcLiMQf0Rf_Wk3V23H2268P_XkPxc.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
On Saturday, Emmanuel Macron, the president of France, announced that Paris would deliver new interceptor missiles to Ukraine as Kyiv’s air defences are running short after the latest round of Russian attacks.
“It is crucial to provide Ukraine with all the necessary means to defend its skies and thwart this aggression,” Mr Macron wrote on X.
He said he had informed Mr Zelensky in a telephone call of “the strengthening of our support with the delivery of interceptors and the continuation of our co-operation”.
Their talks came before a meeting on Monday of Ukraine’s allies in the Coalition of the Willing to look at how to ramp up pressure on Moscow to halt its invasion.
summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky claims that Vladimir Putin plans to draft 300,000 new troops in September following Russia's elections. Concurrently, Ukraine has conducted long-range drone strikes targeting major Russian e-commerce facilities belonging to Ozon and Wildberries to exert economic pressure. Meanwhile, French President Emmanuel Macron announced that Paris will supply new interceptor missiles to support Ukraine's air defenses.
key_points: Volodymyr Zelensky stated that Russia plans to mobilize 300,000 new troops in September, with additional drafts potentially following in 2027.
Zelensky rejected calls from his recently dismissed defense minister to hold wartime elections, warning they pose a severe risk of splitting the country.
Ukraine targeted Ozon and Wildberries logistics facilities with long-range drone strikes to put economic pressure on Moscow.
France announced plans to deliver new interceptor missiles to help replenish Ukraine's depleting air defenses.

title: DR Congo, M23 rebels agree on roadmap for peace talks
author: Al Jazeera Staff
content:
![A member of DRC armed forces stands guard along a street in Sange, South Kivu province](https://www.aljazeera.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/2026-05-13T143803Z_1807338249_RC2O7LA8KFVJ_RTRMADP_3_CONGO-SECURITY-1787462671.jpg?resize=770%2C513&quality=80)
The Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and an M23-led rebel alliance have agreed on a roadmap for peace talks, according to a joint statement, as fighting continues in the country’s east.
The statement on Saturday said the parties had developed a “roadmap setting out sequenced steps and timelines for negotiations” under a framework agreement signed in the Qatari capital, Doha, in November.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3DR Congo to receive 70,000 doses of Ervebo vaccine as Ebola infections surge
- list 2 of 3Ebola outbreak ‘growing faster, wider’ as DRC death toll passes 2,500: UN
- list 3 of 3More than 16,000 doses of Ervebo vaccine arrive in Ebola-hit DR Congo
The roadmap followed five days of talks in Switzerland, from August 17 to August 21 , that also included representatives from the United States, Qatar, Togo, Switzerland and the African Union Commission.
The two sides said they had agreed on “a standardised method for reporting” ceasefire violations and would set up a mechanism to address problems implementing the Doha agreement.
A ceasefire verification mission is due to arrive on Monday in Minembwe, an eastern region in South Kivu province.
Earlier this month, the DRC handed over 15 prisoners to the Congo River Alliance (AFC) and M23 in a transfer facilitated by the International Committee of the Red Cross, as part of the peace process.
Continued fighting
The security situation remains fragile, however, with fighting continuing on the ground.
On Saturday, an AFC/M23 spokesman, Lawrence Kanyuka, claimed that DRC “coalition forces” had launched air raids using kamikaze drones against densely populated areas in the Minembwe region earlier that day.
“These bombings caused civilian casualties and significant damage to civilian infrastructure,” he said in a post on X.
Al Jazeera could not immediately verify the claim.
The United Nations warned in July that the security situation in the provinces of North and South Kivu in the eastern DRC has been further destabilised by the growing use of drones by the warring sides.
An Ebola outbreak in the region has also compounded the crisis, with some 2,500 people having died from the virus since May.
The conflict in the eastern DRC reignited in 2021, when M23 restarted its offensive there. The armed group has since seized swathes of territory, including the provincial capitals of Goma and Bukavu, which were captured in early 2025. The fighting has killed thousands and displaced an estimated 5.3 million people in the region.
The conflict has roots in the 1994 genocide by extremist Hutus against Tutsis in Rwanda and the collapse of the Mobutu Sese Seko government in what was then Zaire.
The DRC, the UN and Western governments have accused Rwanda of backing M23, which is led by ethnic Tutsis, with troops and weapons, but Kigali denies the allegation.
Rwanda in turn accuses DRC of supporting Hutu militias such as the Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Rwanda (FDLR) – a claim Kinshasa denies.
The US brokered a separate peace deal between the DRC and Rwanda last year.
summary: The Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and an M23-led rebel alliance have agreed on a roadmap for peace talks following five days of negotiations in Switzerland. Despite this diplomatic step and an upcoming ceasefire verification mission, fighting continues in the country's eastern region, where the security situation remains fragile. The ongoing conflict, compounded by a severe Ebola outbreak, has resulted in thousands of deaths and millions of displaced people since 2021.
key_points: DRC and the M23 rebel alliance agreed on a roadmap with sequenced steps and timelines for peace negotiations.
The agreement follows five days of talks in Switzerland involving representatives from the US, Qatar, Togo, Switzerland, and the African Union.
Both sides agreed on a standardized method for reporting ceasefire violations and establishing an implementation mechanism.
Fighting continues in eastern DRC, with recent unverified allegations of drone attacks causing civilian casualties in Minembwe.
The broader conflict has killed thousands and displaced an estimated 5.3 million people since M23 restarted its offensive in 2021.

title: ‘No more!!!’: Trump lashes out after US-Canada talks devolve into trade war
author: Lauren Almeida
content:
Donald Trump has hit back at Canada after a breakdown in negotiations plunged the two countries into a trade war.
In his first public comments since negotiations collapsed on Friday in Washington, the US president wrote on social media: “Canada wants the benefits of being a State, without being one!!!”
“They have also charged our great farmers, for many years, massive amounts of tariffs,” he added. “No more!!!”
His comments came after the US imposed 50% tariffs on $20bn (£14.6bn) worth of Canadian goods, while Mark Carney, the country’s prime minister, has vowed to match them “dollar for dollar”.
The US tariffs came into force on Saturday, ranging from hockey sticks to tongue depressors. Trade experts have predicted that the tariffs could result in some job losses, but the biggest impact is expected to be political, triggering fresh tension between the neighbours.
![Canadian trade minister, Dominic LeBlanc, left, and US trade representative Jamieson Greer, speak to reporters in Washington DC on Friday.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/913cad37d9b873ac1107e6b0e217f475077382ec/0_0_1573_1048/master/1573.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Both sides blamed the other for the breakdown in talks on Friday. Carney told Canadian journalists that the country was “at war” over trade with the US, after Trump “miscalculated” by escalating his tariff attack.
“You’re at war when you’re attacked, and we got attacked,” the Canadian prime minister told reporters in Ottawa. “We cannot accept what they’ve offered and we will not give what they’ve asked.”
after newsletter promotion
Jamieson Greer, the US trade representative, has said the US was compelled to act after a year of retaliatory measures by Canada. He told Fox & Friends Weekend: “We’ve said enough and so we’ve taken countermeasures. Our interest is in protecting American workers and protecting American supply chains.”
Carney, who previously served as the governor of the Bank of England, was elected as Canada’s prime minister last year after campaigning to lead a fightback against Trump, who has previously suggested he wants to make Canada a 51st state with “economic force”.
Carney’s “dollar for dollar” tariffs are expected to take effect from 8 September, with new levies on steel, dairy, appliances and electronics. The escalation has also called into question the future of the North American trade pact between the US, Canada and Mexico, known as USMCA.
The pact, which was signed by Trump during his first term, governs about $2tn annually in goods and services between the three countries. Trump refused to renew the USMCA this summer after Canada and Mexico formally requested for it to be renewed for another 16 years.
When asked how the US-Canadian collapse in trade talks would affect the USMCA, Carney said it was “certainly not good news”.
summary: Donald Trump has lashed out at Canada following the collapse of trade negotiations, which resulted in the US imposing 50% tariffs on $20bn worth of Canadian goods. In response, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney vowed to match the tariffs dollar for dollar with levies on steel, dairy, appliances, and electronics. Both leaders blamed each other for the breakdown in talks, raising political tensions and calling into question the future of the USMCA trade pact.
key_points: The US imposed 50% tariffs on $20bn worth of Canadian goods after trade negotiations broke down in Washington.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney vowed to retaliate with dollar-for-dollar tariffs starting September 8.
Donald Trump criticized Canada on social media, accusing them of charging massive tariffs on US farmers and wanting the benefits of statehood without being a state.
The trade escalation has cast doubt on the future of the USMCA trade pact governing goods between the US, Canada, and Mexico.

title: Zelensky vows revenge after Russian attack on shopping mall in his hometown kills 16
author: Rebecca Whittaker
content:
Ukraine’s president Volodymyr Zelensky has vowed to retaliate after a double-tap drone strike on his hometown killed 16 people.
Rescuers are still searching for survivors in the wreckage of a shopping mall in Kryvyi Rih, which was hit twice by Russia on Friday.
More than 130 people were wounded in the daytime attack carried out in two waves, with the second strike targeting emergency workers at the scene of the first.
Zelensky called the attacks an “act of barbarism”, claiming the “absolutely cynical and despicable” second strike was a deliberate attempt to target emergency services.
“Attacks like these are nothing less than terrorist acts,” Zelensky said on Telegram, urging the world to hold Russia to account. “We will definitely respond.”
Regional governor Oleksandr Hanzha said that 22 children were among the wounded and nine people including two children were missing.
“There are 29 people in a serious condition, including five children,” Hanzha said, adding that rescuers were continuing to clear the rubble of the shopping centre.
Rescue teams from four other Ukrainian regions were deployed to help in the search for survivors.
![The mall was hit twice, with the second strike coming half an hour after the first as emergency workers were at the scene](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/08/21/16/2026-08-21T155218Z_1164679702_RC233NA0L0GA_RTRMADP_3_UKRAINE-CRISIS-ATTACK-KRYVYI-RIH.JPG)
Kryvyi Rih mayor Oleksandr Vilkul said the Russian drones were flying at “extremely low altitudes”, describing the attackers as “animals”.
“There are missing people who are not responding to calls,” the mayor added.
Zelensky renewed his calls for more air-defence support following the strikes. In a post on X (Twitter) he said: “Every day that Ukraine lacks sufficient air defence means casualties that could have been prevented.
“Protecting lives requires daily decisions and effective support from the world, and right now, new supplies of ballistic missile interceptors and other missiles can help.”
European Commission vice-president Kaja Kallas called the attack “terror by design”.
She said in a post on X that the strike showed the “absolute and utter depravity of Moscow’s war”.
![Rescuers work at the site of a shopping centre destroyed by Friday's drone attack by Russia](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/08/22/09/2026-08-22T073721Z_74185266_RC2J3NA0KPCW_RTRMADP_3_UKRAINE-CRISIS-ATTACK-KRYVYI-RIH.JPG)
“Russia wants to make Ukrainian cities unliveable,” she added. “I am putting forward the most far-reaching Russia sanctions listings since the start of the war. The pressure must be intensified until Moscow ends the war.”
Kryvyi Rih in particular has been hit multiple times during the war. One of the deadliest occurred in April 2025, when 20 people, including nine children, were killed.
Ms Kallas said EU foreign and defence ministers would discuss how to expand support for Ukraine, including air and missile defence, when they meet in less than two weeks in Dublin.
The attack is the latest in a series of high death toll strikes over the summer.
![The attack is the latest in a series of deadly strikes over the summer](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/08/22/10/2026-08-22T073720Z_1690361237_RC2J3NAMI1TX_RTRMADP_3_UKRAINE-CRISIS-ATTACK-KRYVYI-RIH.JPG)
Friday’s attack came just 24 hours after Russia hit Kyiv with scores of missiles and drones in a nighttime assault that also killed 16 people.
The capital has been hit hard repeatedly in recent weeks: 17 people were killed in a strike on Kyiv and its surrounding region just over two weeks ago; and nine died in another attack on the city two days before that. The United Nations said last week that Kyiv was one of the hardest-hit cities in July, with at least 54 civilians killed and 202 injured.
At the same time, Ukraine has shifted the war onto Russian soil through long-range drone strikes on oil facilities that have caused fuel shortages across the country.
It has also unsettled the Russian public by striking warehouses of Wildberries, the country’s biggest online retailer.
The Russian online news outlet Astra reported on Saturday that a Ukrainian drone set ablaze an oil refinery in the Samara region. Local officials said damage was recorded at an unidentified “industrial facility” and a logistics center for Ozon, a competitor to Wildberries.
summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has vowed to retaliate following a double-tap Russian drone strike on a shopping mall in his hometown of Kryvyi Rih that killed 16 people. The daytime attack injured over 130 people, including 22 children, with a second strike intentionally targeting emergency responders at the scene. In response to the ongoing deadly strikes, Zelensky renewed his calls for increased international air-defense support.
key_points: A double-tap drone strike on a shopping mall in Kryvyi Rih killed 16 people and wounded over 130 others.
The second strike occurred half an hour after the first, deliberately targeting emergency workers at the scene.
President Volodymyr Zelensky condemned the attack as an act of barbarism and vowed to respond.
Zelensky and European officials renewed calls for increased international support and air-defense systems for Ukraine.

title: Carney says new US tariffs are 'designed to hurt us and divide us'
author: Nathan Rennolds
content:
"We cannot accept what they've offered, and we will not give what they've asked," Carney said during a speech outlining Canada's position on the trade dispute with the US.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has hit out at new US tariffs on Canada, saying they were "designed to hurt us and divide us" after talks between Ottawa and Washington broke down on Friday.
Sharing further details on why Canada walked away from what he called a "bad deal," Carney said: "We cannot accept what they've offered, and we will not give what they've asked."
New 50% duties impacting around $20 billion worth of Canadian goods took effect on Saturday after the two countries failed to come to an agreement on a trade deal, with both sides accusing each other of trying to implement last-minute changes.
In a statement on Friday, Carney labelled alleged late changes to the terms of the deal proposed by the US "unfair" and "uneconomic" and said they "called into question the reliability of any deal."
He also warned that Ottawa would match US tariffs "dollar for dollar to protect our workers and businesses."
"Our response will be concentrated in sectors such as steel, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper, and electronics," Carney said in a speech on Saturday.
The Office of the United States Trade Representative has described it as a "missed opportunity" for Canada, which it said was maintaining a "prolonged retaliation" against the US.
"Despite the U.S. offer to Canada to receive the best treatment of any major exporter to our market, new demands and walk backs of other commitments by Canada have upended the careful balance reached in the past days," it added in a statement posted on social media.
The breakdown in talks came despite optimism from US President Donald Trump that a deal could be reached. Trump had postponed the initial planned start date of the tariffs from Wednesday as an agreement appeared near.
Trump, who has repeatedly suggested that Canada should become the US' "51st state," said early on Sunday that Ottawa wanted "the benefits of being a State, without being one."
"They have also charged our great farmers, for many years, massive amounts of Tariffs. No more!!!," he added.
Trump has pursued an aggressive tariff policy since his return to the White House in January 2025, ramping up levies on partners across the world. The administration argues that tariffs will boost US manufacturing and encourage domestic job growth while addressing what it sees as unfair trade rates.
Critics, however, say increasing duties are making life more expensive for American consumers and businesses while fostering widespread uncertainty among companies planning investments and supply chains.
summary: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney criticized new US tariffs as designed to hurt and divide Canada after trade talks between Ottawa and Washington broke down. New 50% duties on approximately $20 billion of Canadian goods took effect after both sides failed to reach an agreement and accused each other of making last-minute changes. In response, Canada has warned that it will match the US tariffs dollar for dollar across targeted sectors such as steel, dairy, and electronics.
key_points: New 50% US tariffs impacting about $20 billion worth of Canadian goods took effect after trade talks collapsed.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney stated that Canada would match the US tariffs dollar for dollar to protect workers and businesses.
Canada's retaliatory measures will focus on sectors including steel, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper, and electronics.
Both Washington and Ottawa blamed each other for introducing last-minute changes that derailed the trade agreement.

title: Russia fires on Kyiv railway in deadly missile attack
author: Lily Shanagher
content:
![Russia's defence ministry said on Saturday that its forces had hit a railway depot](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/world-news/2026/08/22/TELEMMGLPICT000499133579_17873990481400_trans_NvBQzQNjv4Bq7t4Eljyiy6iRMFuEKY2dXA1vLvhkMtVb21dMmpQBfEs.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![Russia's defence ministry said on Saturday that its forces had hit a railway depot](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/world-news/2026/08/22/TELEMMGLPICT000499133579_17873990481400_trans_NvBQzQNjv4Bq7t4Eljyiy6iRMFuEKY2dXA1vLvhkMtVb21dMmpQBfEs.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
At least two people were killed overnight when Russia launched ballistic missiles at a railway in Kyiv.
Oleksandr Pertsovsky, the head of Ukrzaliznytsia, Ukraine’s national rail operator, reported on Saturday that one of the company’s employees had died in the attack on the capital, while Volodymyr Zelensky, Ukraine’s president, said railway infrastructure had been damaged.
Russia’s defence ministry said on Saturday that its forces had hit a railway depot.
Another man was killed and several wounded in a Russian drone strike on Zaporizhzhia, in Ukraine’s south-east, local officials said on Saturday morning.
On Friday, in the central city of Kryvyi Rih, Mr Zelensky’s home town, 16 people were killed and 130 wounded, including 23 children, when Russian drones struck a shopping centre.
Oleksandr Hanzha, the governor of the Dnipropetrovsk region, said in the early hours of Saturday that nine people were missing after the attack.
The daytime strike on the busy shops was condemned as “cynical and despicable” by Mr Zelensky, who shared photos of the aftermath, including a row of body bags.
Footage shared on social media showed the drone soaring through the sky before hitting its target, causing smoke and flames to billow from the building.
Debris and smashed glass surrounded the nearly destroyed shopping centre as injured and bloody survivors were treated on the ground outside.
Kaja Kallas, the EU foreign policy chief, called the attack “terror by design” as she announced “the most far-reaching Russia sanctions listings since the start of the war” before a meeting of the bloc’s foreign ministers in Ireland in September.
Air defence shortage
Russia has intensified its ballistic missile attacks to take advantage of Ukraine’s shortage of US-made Patriot air defence interceptors – the only weapon in its arsenal capable of shooting down such missiles.
Mr Zelensky called on his allies to supply air defences as he discussed the attack on social media, saying: “Every day that Ukraine lacks sufficient air defence means casualties that could have been prevented.
“Protecting lives requires daily decisions and effective support from the world, and right now, new supplies of ballistic missile interceptors and other missiles can help.”
The Ukrainian president said emergency and rescue operations were ongoing at the shopping centre in Kryvyi Rih and that a fire, which spread across 9,000 sq metres, had been extinguished.
![An aerial shot shows fire hoses turned on a large, burning building](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/08/22/TELEMMGLPICT000499072180_17873865528781_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqShPY0ylxE6aYKTx7ZHPuBqaf-kMILQQSjQYZfN-zBD0.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
He added that rescuers from seven regions with search dogs were helping to find people under the rubble.
In Russia, an industrial facility and warehouse were damaged by Ukrainian drones launched overnight.
Vyacheslav Fedorishchev, the governor of the Samara region near Kazan, said that several people had been wounded in the strikes.
He did not identify the facility, but the region has several oil refineries which have been repeatedly attacked by Ukraine.
The warehouse belonged to Ozon, Russia’s second-largest online retailer and rival to Wildberries.
![A firefighter in a smoking, badly damaged building](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/08/22/TELEMMGLPICT000499070725_17873865548930_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqEzw5OF8VsBey80ir11mphkgR7PVUJ79uLnSHs-A1YSI.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
The company said that work at its Samara region logistics centre in the town of Chapayevsk had been halted after the strike, which it said caused injuries.
The strike was the first on Ozon, after Kyiv spent weeks targeting Wildberries, casting the company as part of its wider campaign against the economic infrastructure underpinning Russia’s military campaign.
The strikes have unsettled the Russian public, as Kyiv shows its ability to attack the heart of the country with long-range drones.
Russia’s defence ministry said it had downed 457 Ukrainian drones overnight.
summary: Russian ballistic missile and drone attacks targeted multiple Ukrainian locations, including a railway in Kyiv and a shopping centre in Kryvyi Rih, resulting in multiple deaths and injuries. President Volodymyr Zelensky urged allies to provide urgent air defense supplies amid a shortage of interceptors. Meanwhile, Ukrainian drone strikes damaged an industrial facility and an Ozon warehouse in Russia's Samara region.
key_points: At least two people were killed in a ballistic missile attack on a Kyiv railway.
A Russian drone strike on a shopping centre in Kryvyi Rih killed 16 people and wounded 130.
President Zelensky called on international allies to supply more air defense systems.
Ukrainian drones damaged an industrial facility and an Ozon warehouse in Russia's Samara region.

title: Sydney Swans fans turn out in record numbers for AFLW match but hundreds walk out before men’s fixture
author: Jack Larkin
content:
Some Sydney Swans fans have walked out of the Sydney Cricket Ground in protest during a historic double-header amid a scandal that has shaken Australian football.
Five AFL players – Isaac Heeney, Nick Blakey, Chad Warner, Riley Bice and James Jordon – have been stood down for the rest of the season by the Swans for breaching the club’s standards, including drinking and bringing women back to their hotel after their round 23 win over Essendon.
Victoria police are investigating an alleged sexual assault early on 17 August at a Pullman hotel in East Melbourne, where the Sydney Swans were staying.
Sydney’s AFLW side took on Essendon on Sunday at the SCG before the men’s side closed out its regular season against North Melbourne.
But after the women’s team beat the Bombers by 24 points, hundreds of Swans fans streamed out before the AFL clash.
In the lead-up, some lifelong Swans fans were wrestling with whether to show their support for the men’s side.
Shayal, a Swans member, said she felt a sombre mood on the light rail heading to the game, adding that she would be leaving after the women’s match.
“I’m only planning to stay for the women’s game and then leaving before the men’s game,” she said.
“I’ve been a member for over 10 years, and it just doesn’t feel right. And I’m not sure if I’ll renew my membership again.”
![Sydney Swans fans seen leaving the SCG after the AFLW side beat Essendon on Sunday](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/78ff113a6a8cd7e19914685bc89604c83b0c085a/0_0_4558_3646/master/4558.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Other fans said they still supported the club despite feeling disappointed in the players who were stood down.
Daniel, a member for 26 years, said he would be staying for both games.
“I will be watching both. It’s ultimately a club. It’s ultimately both teams,” he said. “I think it’s the fact that those five players are not out there which made me comfortable to stay to watch the men’s game.”
Swans fan Kate Hipsley also said she wouldn’t be walking out.
“As far as we know, the men playing in the men’s game have not done anything wrong and they will be hurting as well,” she said.
![Swans players huddle during the round two AFLW match against Essendon](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/71eba0e7c913fe7a7935789c0262c337b0add182/0_0_2401_1600/master/2401.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
The match drew a record AFLW crowd for the Swans, with 16,672 people watching on. It was the first time Sydney’s AFLW and AFL teams have shared a double-header at the SCG.
None of the Swans AFL players who were stood down have been arrested or charged, and much about the allegations remains unknown.
The five players apologised in relation to the club sanctions in a joint statement issued by the Swans on Wednesday. “We are deeply sorry to everyone involved,” they said. “We know that our behaviour has fallen well short of the standards expected of us and the values of our club.”
Inside the SCG on Sunday, Swans fans made a special effort to loudly cheer every goal, positive play or desperate act from their AFLW team.
![People walking out before the Swans’ men’s team played at the SCG on Sunday](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/589ae2670c5e2e7687e0c86dc8e0e10e6672f716/698_0_4191_3355/master/4191.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
But the merchandise stands and fan gear worn by supporters watching the women play were a reminder of what happened off the field this week. 
 There was no sign of Swans star Heeney, or popular players including Warner and Blakey, on merchandise for sale or on T-shirts and hats worn by fans dressed in red and white.
Large posters around the stands that would usually feature Heeney heavily have been covered by posters focused on men’s captain Callum Mills or simply “SWANS” in large font.
Some Swans fans held signs supporting women, including one that read: “The Swans are nothing without W.”
![Swans supporters at the SCG on Sunday.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/e0c4b903b67aa6690c4b27cbb6bb4b3f8cd7b8c9/0_0_6516_4344/master/6516.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
A banner that read “no more dickheads please” was removed from a stand by SCG security during the AFLW game. The banner appeared to reference Sydney’s “no dickheads” recruiting policy during the time when Paul Roos was coach, part of the club’s renowned “bloods culture”.
The club’s turmoil did appear to affect the turnout for the men’s match, and the usual parochial cheers were replaced by polite applause as the Sydney players ran out to face North Melbourne.
The Swans have averaged 36,367 fans at their previous 11 home games at the SCG this year, but the number of vacant seats deep into the first term suggested the level of support had fallen away after a tumultuous week. The official crowd for the men’s match was 30,058, Sydney’s smallest crowd at the SCG this season.
Sydney were too strong for the Kangaroos, storming home in the last quarter to win by 53 points. There were emotional scenes after match, with a number of Swans wiping away tears, including captain Callum Mills and midfielder Errol Gulden.
Additional reporting by Martin Pegan and Australian Associated Press
summary: Hundreds of Sydney Swans fans walked out of the Sydney Cricket Ground after a record-breaking AFLW match in protest during the club's ongoing scandal. Five male AFL players were stood down for the rest of the season following a breach of club standards and an alleged sexual assault investigation by Victoria police. Despite the controversy and a reduced crowd for the men's fixture against North Melbourne, the Swans went on to win the match by 53 points.
key_points: Five Sydney Swans players were stood down for the remainder of the season for drinking and bringing women back to their hotel.
Victoria police are investigating an alleged sexual assault at a Melbourne hotel where the team stayed.
A record AFLW crowd of 16,672 watched Sydney beat Essendon, but hundreds of fans left before the men's game against North Melbourne.
The official crowd for the men's match was 30,058, marking Sydney's smallest home crowd of the season.

title: The ‘ordinary’ woman accused of assassinating a Russian commander in Crimea
author: Pjotr Sauer
content:
It was just after dawn in Sevastopol when a powerful explosion tore through a quiet square in a residential district of the Russian-occupied Crimean port city.
Hidden inside a rubbish bin, a bomb containing the equivalent of about 500g of TNT detonated on 13 August as Robert Shageev, the deputy commander of a Russian Black Sea fleet submarine brigade, walked past in naval uniform. He was killed on the spot.
Within hours, investigators had a suspect. Police detained Margarita Reutt, a 32-year-old resident of Sochi, the Russian resort city about 300 miles across the Black Sea from Sevastopol.
During a search, investigators said they had found a remote control they believed was used to detonate the bomb that killed Shageev, a former commander of Ukraine’s only submarine who switched allegiance to Russia in 2014 when Moscow annexed Crimea.
According to the security service, she confessed to the attack and said that a handler linked to Ukrainian intelligence had promised her a large payment in cryptocurrency and documents that would allow her to leave Russia afterwards.
![Margarita Reutt standing on a stone with a view of a river and mountains](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/3ffc50fb09085423a9c1081c1515f14d8128614d/0_150_1360_1290/master/1360.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
The FSB also said Reutt showed no remorse.
Those assertions could not be independently verified, and Russian security agencies have previously publicised purported confessions from detainees before their cases have reached court. But several people previously accused by Russia of carrying out similar attacks against military figures were later found by reporters to have been involved in the operations Moscow had accused them of conducting.
What exactly drove Reutt to allegedly embark on such an audacious mission remains unclear. As with other cases involving accused Ukrainian intelligence operations, her trial is likely to take place behind closed doors, offering little opportunity for her to give her own account publicly.
But interviews with a dozen friends and acquaintances, combined with an examination of years of her social media activity, offer a portrait of a determined and adventurous woman whose attitude towards her country appears to have hardened gradually, with signs of a more striking change emerging in the months leading up to the attack.
“Rita believed that the country was going in the wrong direction,” said a longtime friend, using the diminutive form of her name. “But I am still shocked she went so far,” the friend added.
![Margarita Reutt sits on a stool in a posed photograph.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/3c3117e99bc7f9e822d486de92557d57c0aa76d2/0_0_1920_2560/master/1920.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Russia quickly accused Reutt of carrying out the attack on the orders of Ukrainian intelligence. Kyiv has not commented on the bombing or Reutt’s alleged role in it.
Since the start of the full-scale invasion, Ukraine’s intelligence agencies have been linked to a string of assassinations and attempted killings of senior Russian military officers whom Kyiv has accused of involvement in the invasion. Ukrainian officials have occasionally acknowledged involvement in such operations, but more often have remained silent.
The attacks have involved an array of methods and recruits, from committed anti-Kremlin saboteurs to Russians promised large sums of money. In other cases, unsuspecting couriers and delivery workers have effectively been used as mules.
Usually, little is known about those accused of carrying out such attacks or how they prepared for them. Some have managed to escape, or were never publicly identified by Russian authorities, while others were killed carrying out their operations.
The swift capture and naming of Reutt, however, offers a rare opportunity to examine the journey of a Russian citizen accused of turning against her own country.
Reutt, born Margarita Yakovleva, grew up in Yaroslavl, a city north-east of Moscow, where she took the surname of the grandmother who largely raised her after her parents divorced. Friends recalled a largely unremarkable childhood, remembering her as warm and sociable, but also unusually drawn to adventure and risk.
“Margarita was fearless. She would climb trees, jump off cars, do things most boys were scared of,” recalled one friend from her childhood.
That streak followed her to Novosibirsk, thousands of miles to the east, where she studied management and threw herself into university life. Reutt became a regular at a local parachuting club, with photographs showing her jumping from Soviet-era aircraft, often the only woman among groups of men in camouflage gear.
She also won prizes in amateur go-karting competitions and took up water polo, becoming goalkeeper for the university team and quickly distinguishing herself despite being new to the sport. “Margarita was so talented and never afraid of the ball,” recalled her water polo coach at the time.
There was little then to suggest hostility towards the Kremlin. In Novosibirsk, Reutt became a well-liked member of a patriotic volunteer group that searched for the remains of Soviet soldiers killed during the second world war, part of a nationwide movement dedicated to recovering and reburying the war dead.
After graduating, Reutt moved south to Sochi, the Black Sea resort that became her home. She briefly tried her hand at running a travel agency before joining Vitauct in the early 2020s, an alternative medicine company specialising in longevity.
“She was the most ordinary person,” said Gennadiy Garbuzov, the company’s founder, who struggled to reconcile the woman he knew with the allegations now facing her. “There was nothing to indicate she would do this. She must have fallen under someone’s influence.”
On the surface, her online life was similarly unremarkable. She posted frequently about health and animal rights and took to Telegram forums to discuss alternative medicine.
Reutt also travelled widely. Leaked records from travel databases seen by the Guardian and photographs posted online show frequent trips abroad, including to Turkey, Thailand and Sri Lanka, where she often shared photographs of herself in bikinis at beach resorts.
![Margarita Reutt in a white swimsuit.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/7aa1595975fb9cd60e5059ed0057b261df09739f/0_0_2560_1920/master/2560.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
“Margarita just seemed to be living her life and had lots of plans for the future,” said another colleague at Vitauct.
“She was good-looking and popular,” the colleague added.
In October 2025, Reutt travelled to Minsk for her sister’s wedding. Photographs from the celebration show her smiling among relatives and catching the bridal bouquet. To one friend she painted an idyllic picture of her life in Sochi, traversing mountains, waterfalls and canyons. “You can explore endlessly here, everything is lush and green,” she wrote to the friend.
But beneath that outwardly happy life, another side of Reutt was becoming visible. She increasingly expressed concerns about environmental problems plaguing Sochi, and started to become involved in local volunteer initiatives, friends said.
After a large oil spill in the Black Sea in December 2024, when two Russian tankers were wrecked in a storm, Reutt travelled to Anapa to join volunteers cleaning mazut, a heavy fuel oil, from contaminated beaches.
Exactly when dissatisfaction with her surroundings hardened into something more political is difficult to establish. Friends described a growing estrangement from Russia that deepened after the country launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
“The war came as a shock,” said one friend, who recalled Reutt becoming increasingly outspoken in public about the fighting in Ukraine. “I told her once to keep quiet, otherwise she would get us both into trouble,” the friend said.
By July 2025, her anti-war feelings had spilt into public view. While travelling on a Samara-Adler train, Reutt was fined under Russia’s sweeping law against “discrediting” the armed forces after reportedly shouting “Serves you right, Russians!” when news broke of a Ukrainian drone strike on a railway station in the Rostov region.
The following February, Reutt posted the results of a genetic test showing she was 98% Russian, adding a hashtag declaring that she was “ashamed to be Russian”.
Yet to friends and acquaintances, Reutt appeared to carry on much as before. She picked up occasional jobs, appeared in video clips made by friends and continued to travel. As recently as March, photographs from a trip to Cuba showed her drinking from a coconut.
![Margarita Reutt on a beach in Cuba.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/340668420c17e9fb796b946262330e30bcd3a65f/0_391_1928_1638/master/1928.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
It was only in late spring, several people who knew her said, that her behaviour began to change in ways they struggled to understand at the time. “She became more withdrawn,” recalled one friend.
Around the same time, a group of friends began planning a trip together for the autumn. Reutt declined to join them without much explanation – an unusual response from someone friends said could be counted on to say yes to a new adventure.
Another friend remembered Reutt suddenly acquiring a second phone. “She bought this second phone in the spring. She explained that she needed it for work, but it didn’t really make sense to me at the time.”
“Margarita was hiding something,” the friend added. “I thought maybe she had a new boyfriend.”
By the summer, Reutt had begun spending more time in Crimea, the place where she would eventually be arrested. One acquaintance said she explained the trips to Crimea by saying she was scouting possible locations for video shoots, having recently begun appearing more frequently in music clips.
What she was actually doing in Crimea – and when, if at all, she came into contact with Ukrainian intelligence – remains unknown.
If Russia’s allegations that she was recruited by Ukraine are true, Reutt would join a growing group of Russian citizens accused of being enlisted by Ukrainian intelligence to carry out sabotage and assassinations deep behind the frontlines.
Such recruits offer obvious advantages: they can move around Russia more freely, and attract less scrutiny than Ukrainian operatives, and they can reach targets far from the frontline without putting trained agents at risk. Women have featured prominently in several of the most high-profile operations, potentially attracting even less suspicion.
For those close to Reutt, there is no easy explanation for how the woman they remember ended up accused of carrying out an assassination. But a friend of two decades recalled a stubborn determination to follow through on whatever she decided to do.
“If she had a plan in mind, she would do it,” the friend said. “Even if it was something like this.”
summary: Margarita Reutt, a 32-year-old Russian woman from Sochi, was detained and accused by Russian investigators of assassinating Robert Shageev, a deputy commander of a Russian Black Sea fleet submarine brigade, in Sevastopol using a remote-controlled bomb. According to the FSB, Reutt confessed that she was promised a large cryptocurrency payment and travel documents by a Ukrainian intelligence handler. While friends and acquaintances described her as an ordinary and adventurous person, her social media and personal life revealed a growing disillusionment with the Russian government and the war in Ukraine.
key_points: Robert Shageev, a senior Russian naval officer, was killed on August 13 by an explosion from a bomb hidden in a rubbish bin in Sevastopol, Crimea.
Russian authorities detained Margarita Reutt as a suspect, stating they found a remote control used to detonate the bomb and that she confessed to acting on behalf of Ukrainian intelligence.
