Kyiv has not commented on the bombing or Reutt's alleged involvement.

Friends and acquaintances noted that Reutt's attitude toward Russia hardened significantly following the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, culminating in anti-war statements and a fine for discrediting the armed forces.

title: Another Democratic rising star jibes at Trump over close aide Natalie Harp
author: Bruce Golding
content:
Progressive Democrat Abdul El-Sayed became the second Senate candidate to invoke the controversy surrounding President Donald Trump’s relationship with embattled White House aide Natalie Harp — telling her on social media Saturday that her 80-year-old boss “needs his rest.”
The combined shots at Trump and his 35-year-old assistant came as a new report said Harp posted in support of Trump more than 150 times on January 6, 2021, when MAGA loyalists stormed the U.S. Capitol in a bid to keep Congress from certifying his election loss to Joe Biden.
El-Sayed, the Democratic Senate candidate from Michigan, mocked the aging president's stamina after Trump on Friday accused him of having “recently campaigned with a communist fanatic who says that America deserved 9/11,” an apparent reference to progressive influencer Hasan Piker.
“Natalie, I think he's had a little too much iPad for the week. He needs his rest,” El-Sayed quipped.
![White House aide Natalie Harp reportedly wrote more than 150 since-deleted social media posts in support of President Donald Trump on January 6, 2021](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/08/18/16/34/GettyImages-2287538819.jpg)
It follows a dig from Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff of Georgia, whose comments thrust Harp, a former far-right cable TV host and 2024 Trump campaign staffer, into the spotlight and sparked heated reactions from the White House.
He alluded to Harp’s relationship with the president during an August 16 re-election campaign rally, and accused Trump of not wanting to “do the job” of president. “He wants to build his ballroom and travel with Natalie,” Ossoff said.
Also Saturday, CNN said it had uncovered scores of posts Harp made on Twitter, now known as X, before her account was apparently suspended.
They included repeated exhortations made January 6 to "FIGHT FOR TRUMP!" according to a screenshot CNN included in its report.
Harp's since-deleted posts also reportedly told Trump, “We love you” and included an altered version of Psalm 43:1 that asked God to vindicate Trump and rescue him “from those who are deceitful and wicked.”
The White House didn't immediately respond to a Saturday afternoon inquiry from The Independent.
![Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed poked at Trump after the president accused him of having ‘recently campaigned with a communist fanatic’](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/08/10/00/2026-08-08T024105Z_2116461374_RC2ZTMA7LGWS_RTRMADP_3_USA-ELECTON-MICHIGAN.JPG)
Ossoff’s crack came after CNN revealed that Harp was among three White House aides who flew with Trump from Turkey to the U.K. on a military jet after he was snuck off Air Force One in response to an Iranian assassination threat.
Unknowing journalists and other members of Trump's administration, including Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, made the trip on the presidential decoy plane.
Democratic strategists were divided over Ossoff's remark, with Anthony Coley, a former Department of Justice spokesperson, telling The Hill, “Timing matters enormously in politics, and Ossoff caught this wave at exactly the right moment.”
Democratic strategist Joel Payne also credited Ossoff with successfully questioning the president's priorities, saying that “if you can make that point with a little bit of hot sauce on top of it, I think that makes for effective politics.”
But David Axelrod, chief strategist for President Barack Obama's winning 2008 and 2012 campaigns, said on social media that the two words Ossoff used to mention Harp “seemed gratuitous and unnecessary.”
“Probably thrilled some in the base, who figured it was just giving Trump a taste of his own nasty medicine. But they distracted and detracted from the power of the message,” Axelrod added.
Harp worked in the White House for more than a year without seeking a security clearance normally obtained by West Wing staffers, MS NOW reported Wednesday, citing two unidentified people familiar with the matter.
It's unclear why Harp didn't apply for the clearance, but she's since filled out the necessary forms at Trump's request after the White House counsel's office and national security officials raised concerns, MS NOW said.
summary: Progressive Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed mocked President Donald Trump and White House aide Natalie Harp on social media, telling her that the president "needs his rest." This follows a similar jab from Senator Jon Ossoff regarding Trump's relationship with Harp, a former campaign staffer and cable host. Meanwhile, a CNN report revealed that Harp posted in support of Trump more than 150 times on January 6, 2021, while another report noted she worked in the White House for over a year without seeking a standard security clearance.
key_points: Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed mocked President Trump's stamina and his relationship with aide Natalie Harp on social media.
Senator Jon Ossoff previously drew attention to Harp during a campaign rally, accusing Trump of traveling with her instead of doing the job.
A CNN report uncovered that Harp made more than 150 posts in support of Trump on January 6, 2021.
Reports indicated that Harp worked in the White House for over a year before finally filling out security clearance forms at Trump's request.

title: Iran’s new security chief says neighbours who join US economic war will be considered ‘enemies’
author: Staff; Agencies; Guardian staff reporter
content:
The new leader of Iran’s top security body has warned its neighbours against joining new US efforts to squeeze Tehran’s economy, and threatened US commercial interests in the region, as Donald Trump doubled down on his fanciful view that the strait of Hormuz was a new US territory.
Mohsen Rezaei, the hardline new leader of Iran’s supreme national security council, told state television that Iran would target oil-shipping routes out the Gulf – alternatives to the strait of Hormuz – if its neighbours joined what he called the “economic war” waged by the US. Those neighbours would be “considered an enemy” and “we will target their interests”, he said.
Rezaei was a commander-in-chief of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) for most of the 1980-88 war with Iraq and was named this month in a series of senior appointments widely seen as hardening Tehran’s political and military stance.
His interview with broadcaster IRIB is his most extensive public statement since his appointment.
Rezaei also claimed the Islamic republic had more cards to play in the war, saying “we have not yet attacked any American economic interests”.
“So far, we have only targeted military bases, but if they want to impose economic sanctions on us, the United States has oil and economic companies around Iran and elsewhere, and we will strike them,” Rezai said in the interview, broadcast on Saturday.
Last week, Trump announced a new campaign to isolate Iran’s economy, threatening “tremendous economic consequences” on any country that helps or does business with Tehran, as the US president’s unpopular war drags toward the six-month mark without any significant sign of resolution.
Trump’s efforts to finish the war he started along with Israel on 28 February have foundered after a ceasefire agreement signed in June collapsed – leaving Iran in control of the strait of Hormuz, a waterway that was the conduit for one-fifth of the world’s oil supplies before the conflict.
Washington has called on other governments to join its efforts to isolate the Iranian economy, notably China, among Iran’s top strategic partners. However Beijing has criticised the initiative, arguing that US sanctions would not resolve the conflict in the Middle East.
One of Iran’s major trading partners, the United Arab Emirates, announced on Tuesday last week that it was suspending all trade and financial transactions with Tehran until further notice.
The US treasury has for months been carrying out Operation Economic Fury, aiming to cut off Iran’s funding with targeted sanctions, while a naval blockade in the strait of Hormuz has sought to block Iranian ports from exporting oil vital to keeping the country’s economy afloat.
The US president has in recent days repeatedly raised the concept of declaring the strait a US territory. “We control it with the blockade, and I like the idea of declaring it a territory,” he told reporters on Monday when asked about that comment.
On Friday, the US president told a crowd in South Carolina: “We don’t even know if we won, because I view the strait of Hormuz as an American territory right now.”
On Saturday night, Trump again shared on his social media platform a map graphic showing the Gulf and describing the strait of Hormuz as a “new US territory”.
Rezaei said in his interview that discussions continued with cross-strait neighbour Oman over management of the waterway, and said fees would be imposed.
French president Emmanuel Macron and Saudi crown prince Mohammed bin Salman are expected to discuss plans to develop alternative routes to the strait of Hormuz during the Saudi leader’s two-day visit to Paris that starts on Sunday, according to officials in the presidency who weren’t authorised to speak publicly.
Proposals include increasing trade through Omani ports outside the Gulf, expanding or doubling pipelines in Saudi Arabia and elsewhere, and developing new rail links, the officials said.
France and Saudi Arabia have formed a taskforce on energy and logistics connections between the Middle East and Europe that is scheduled to meet at the ministerial level on Monday. The officials said the work would focus on identifying the most strategic projects, securing financing and establishing roles for French companies.
With Associated Press and Agence France-Presse
summary: Mohsen Rezaei, the new leader of Iran’s supreme national security council, warned regional neighbors that joining US economic sanctions against Tehran will result in them being treated as enemies whose interests will be targeted. The threat comes in response to a new US campaign led by Donald Trump to isolate Iran's economy and assert control over the strait of Hormuz. Meanwhile, international partners like France and Saudi Arabia are discussing alternative trade and energy routes to bypass the contested waterway.
key_points: Iran threatened to treat regional neighbors as enemies and target their interests if they participate in US economic warfare.
Mohsen Rezaei stated that Iran could begin striking US economic and oil companies in the region.
President Donald Trump announced a new campaign to isolate Iran's economy and referred to the strait of Hormuz as a US territory.
France and Saudi Arabia are discussing plans to develop alternative trade routes and pipelines to bypass the strait of Hormuz.

title: Trump brags over ballroom after court allows construction to continue – for now
author: Ariana Baio
content:
President Donald Trump gloated over the rapid progress being made on the White House ballroom, less than a day after the Supreme Court said that he could continue building the vast structure - for now.
The president posted a photo Saturday morning on Truth Social of the first floor nearing completion with walls rising on the second floor. In the background, the White House can be seen, dwarfed by the 90,000 square-foot structure.
“Tremendous work has been done on the magnificent BALLROOM/MILITARY COMPLEX being built on the grounds of the White House!” Trump wrote. “Presidents have wanted this for 150 years, and so has everyone else.”
He also boasted the project “will be paid for with ZERO Dollars of Taxpayer Money” – a claim disputed by Washington Post reporting which found that the administration was using more than $300 million from taxpayer-funded departments and agencies to pay for parts of the ballroom.
Trump has become fixated on the ballroom project in his second term with repeated posts on Truth Social, and press conferences and interviews disgressing into the topic.
![President Trump posted a photo on Truth Social Saturday morning showing off construction of the White House ballroom](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/08/22/16/06/16a724c8d949a6d1.jpg)
The proposed ballroom has met with pushback from groups, including the National Trust for Historic Preservation, a nonprofit, which sued to stop its construction. The group claims the president must obtain congressional approval first.
But after two lower courts ruled in favor of the trust and ordered Trump to halt above-ground construction until Congress approves it, the Supreme Court stepped in Friday to side with the president.
In the court order, Chief Justice John Roberts allowed the Trump administration to temporarily continue construction on the project while the justices consider intervening in the ongoing lawsuit. As is typical with emergency orders, Roberts did not explain why he was allowing Trump to continue construction.
The Trump administration has argued the ballroom is necessary for national security purposes because it sits above a sprawling underground bunker, containing a medical facility and emergency operations center and below a drone-proof roof.
![President Trump has been fixated on his White House ballroom project, constantly bringing it up in social media posts, during unrelated press conferences and arguing it’s critical for national security purposes](<https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/08/07/15/11/GettyImages-2242296293-(1).jpg>)
Lower courts have said the national security-related construction can continue, but the ballroom itself needs approval from Congress. However, the administration argues it’s all related to national security.
Despite Trump’s consistent claims that his ballroom is fulfilling long-held wishes for past presidents and others, a July poll from the Washington Post/Ipsos found that 65 percent of U.S. adults said they were dissatisfied or upset with Trump’s renovation projects.
The ballroom is just one of several projects the president has undertaken in his second term.
Trump has bragged about repairing, restoring and cleaning monuments and statues around the nation’s capital. He boasted about renovating the bathroom attached to the Lincoln Bedroom in the White House, showing off the new gilded and white marble room.
The president is also pushing to build a triumphal arch in Washington, D.C., to mark America’s 250th anniversary.
Like his ballroom, the president has also been fixated on restoring the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, taking credit for fixing it and then blaming others after those repairs failed. The administration even pressed prosecutors to bring charges against people for vandalizing the pool – charges that were later dropped due to lack of evidence.
summary: President Donald Trump celebrated rapid construction progress on the massive White House ballroom project after the Supreme Court temporarily allowed building to continue. Trump claimed the project requires no taxpayer money, though reporting indicates the administration is using over $300 million from taxpayer-funded departments. The project faces legal challenges from groups like the National Trust for Historic Preservation, which argues congressional approval is needed, while the administration maintains the structure is necessary for national security.
key_points: The Supreme Court allowed construction of the White House ballroom to temporarily continue while considering an ongoing lawsuit.
Trump boasted on Truth Social about the progress and claimed the project uses zero taxpayer dollars, a claim disputed by reporting.
The National Trust for Historic Preservation sued to stop construction, arguing the project requires congressional approval.
The administration defends the ballroom as a national security necessity because it sits above an underground bunker and features a drone-proof roof.
A July Washington Post/Ipsos poll showed 65 percent of U.S. adults were dissatisfied or upset with Trump's renovation projects.

title: Ukraine war live: Putin pulls ambassador from London
author: Rebecca Whittaker; Nicole Wootton-Cane
content:
Vladimir Putin has reportedly pulled Russia’s ambassador from London, accusing Britain of taking the “path of confrontation”.
Andrey Kelin, who served as the Russian ambassador to the UK for over seven years, vacated his post on 21 July, reports The Times. It is understood that Moscow has not sought to appoint a replacement amid fears of a diplomatic breakdown.
It comes after prime minister Andy Burnham said the UK is continuing to “support Ukraine 100 per cent” after Moscow threatened consequences for the reported use of British drones for strikes deep into Russia.
On Saturday, Mr Putin warned Kyiv has “opened Pandora’s box” after a campaign of Ukrainian strikes killed at least 10 people in Russia. Ukrainian drones hit an oil refinery, as well as a warehouse belonging to major Russian online retailer, Ozon.
The strikes came one day after after Putin’s shopping centre strike killed 16 people and wounded more than 130 others.
President Volodymyr Zelensky promised a response to the attack, which he described as an "act of barbarism".
Watch: Huge queues and fighting at pumps as Putin threatens to arrest Russians complaining about fuel shortages
Russians ‘withdraw billions from banks over fears Putin will seize deposits for war’
Russian citizens are withdrawing billions of roubles from the country’s banks over fears that the Kremlin could seize deposits to fund the war in Ukraine.
Analysts say fears that the Kremlin could confiscate private savings to bankroll the conflict have triggered widespread panic, with more than 286.4bn roubles (£2.5bn) pulled from Russian banks during the first two weeks of August alone.
A staggering £5.3bn was reported to have been withdrawn in July on top of a further £3.32bn in June, according to Central Bank data.
Taras Skvortsov, an executive at state-owned Sberbank, has warned that total capital flight this year could be double what was seen during the initial months of Russia’s 2022 invasion.
You can read the full report below:
‘Putin has repeatedly threatened the UK and Nato over Ukraine – but he is too weak to follow through’
Putin’s posturing is a poor attempt to scare off broader Western support for Kyiv, say experts. Suha Kidwai reports.
In pictures: Ukrainians rally to mark their National Flag Day in Istanbul
![A Ukrainian woman wearing a T-shirt with a printed picture of a missing Ukrainian soldier on the back](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/08/22/18/2026-08-22T153205Z_2102492310_RC2R3NA0HC35_RTRMADP_3_UKRAINE-CRISIS-FLAG-DAY-TURKEY.JPG)
![A Ukrainian woman living in Turkey holds balloons in colors of the Ukrainian flag](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/08/22/18/2026-08-22T152706Z_651798997_RC2R3NAEMJH7_RTRMADP_3_UKRAINE-CRISIS-FLAG-DAY-TURKEY.JPG)
![A Ukrainian boy living in Turkey holds a portrait of a missing soldier](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/08/22/18/2026-08-22T152837Z_556454313_RC2R3NA4I675_RTRMADP_3_UKRAINE-CRISIS-FLAG-DAY-TURKEY.JPG)
Putin pulls ambassador from London amid fears of breakdown in diplomatic relations
Vladimir Putin has reportedly pulled Russia’s long-serving UK ambassador from London amid fears of a diplomatic breakdown between Moscow and the UK.
The Times reported on Saturday night that Andrey Kelin vacated his post on 21 July. No replacement has been sought by Moscow.
A spokesman for the Russian embassy told The Times Mr Kelin had made “considerable efforts to preserve contacts and channels of communication” with the UK and accused the government of choosing a “path of confrontation” with Russia.
![Ambassador of the Russian Federation to the UK Andrei Kelin left his post in July (Aaron Chown/PA)](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/06/03/15/273cff6b339fdfdac067c8d10427cb59Y29udGVudHNlYXJjaGFwaSwxNzgwNTc5MDY1-2.65455227.jpg)
Putin says Ukraine has opened 'Pandora's box' over strikes
Vladimir Putin has said Ukraine has “opened Pandora’s box” after hitting Russian targets in a string of drone strikes on Saturday.
Russia and Ukraine are both ramping up drone campaigns aiming to cripple each other's economic infrastructure, often striking targets far beyond the war's front lines, as fighting on the battlefield grinds toward the 4-and-a-half-year mark.
On Friday, at least 16 people were killed and more than 130 wounded when several Russian drones struck a shopping centre in central Ukraine. Russian President Vladimir Putin said on Saturday that Ukraine's strikes, which Kyiv says seek to choke off financing for Moscow's war effort, had opened a "Pandora's box" of Russian retaliation.
Putin arrests Russians for complaining about fuel shortages as fighting breaks out at petrol stations
Russian police have arrested citizens complaining of fuel shortages at the pump, as Ukraine’s drone campaign sparked fighting at petrol stations and rationing.
Moscow and its surrounding regions have been forced to reimpose purchase limits on fuel, capping sales at between 50 and 60 litres per vehicle.
As Ukraine intensifies its “deep strike” campaign, hitting another major oil refinery on Wednesday, the strain on Russia’s domestic energy grid continues to grow. Across at least 12 regions, miles of gridlocked traffic now stall forecourts, with motorists waiting up to 30 hours only to find the pumps empty.
The prolonged waits have pushed the Russian public to breaking point, with footage showing fights erupting between drivers over fuel.
You can read the full story below:
![](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/08/20/13/56/Screenshot-2026-08-20-at-14-49-31.png?trim=0,175,0,175&width=1200&height=800&crop=1200:800)
US Army to shut down unit in Europe focused on drone warfare in latest shakeup
A drone warfareUS Army unit in Europe has been told to return to being a traditional infantry battalion.
For more nearly a year, soldiers of the 173rd Airborne Brigade have been experimenting and building their own drones, as well as participating in drills on waging unmanned warfare after Ukraine pioneered such tactics in its yearslong conflict with Russia.
Pictured: Trucks on fire following strike on Kyiv
Two trucks caught fire during a Russian strike on Kyiv.
Two people have been killed and nine others are injured following the attack this afternoon.
![](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/08/22/13/2026-08-22T113244Z_1758765344_RC2N3NAGT7FU_RTRMADP_3_UKRAINE-CRISIS-ATTACK-KYIV-REGION.JPG)
summary: Russian President Vladimir Putin has withdrawn Russia's ambassador to the UK, Andrey Kelin, amid worsening diplomatic relations and accusations that Britain has chosen a path of confrontation. The move coincides with escalating drone strikes between Russia and Ukraine targeting critical economic infrastructure. Meanwhile, Russian citizens are withdrawing billions of roubles from banks over fears of deposit seizures, and severe fuel shortages are prompting panic, rationing, and arrests across Russia.
key_points: Russian ambassador to the UK Andrey Kelin vacated his post on 21 July, with Moscow appointing no replacement.
Vladimir Putin warned that Ukraine opened Pandora's box following a campaign of drone strikes that killed at least 10 people in Russia.
Russian citizens withdrew billions of roubles from banks amid fears that the Kremlin might seize private deposits to fund the war.
Fuel shortages and purchase caps in Russia have sparked gridlocked traffic, fighting at petrol stations, and arrests of complaining citizens.

title: Donald Trump teases Natalie Harp for Press Secretary role after Leavitt exit
author: Owen Scott
content:
Trump joked Natalie Harp could replace Karoline Leavitt as White House press secretary: report
![Trump joked Natalie Harp could replace Karoline Leavitt as White House press secretary: report](<https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/08/21/9/32/Karoline-Leavitt-Natalie-Harp.jpeg?quality=75&width=83&auto=webp 83w>)
Donald Trump teases Natalie Harp for Press Secretary role after Leavitt exit
- Donald Trump reportedly joked that his executive assistant, Natalie Harp, could replace outgoing White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt following her unexpected departure announcement.
- Harp, known for providing Trump with printed news and social media posts, has recently faced increased scrutiny over her close role in the administration.
- Trump posted an AI-generated image of himself at the White House press briefing room podium with the caption "The Best Press Secretary."
- Political commentator Scott Jennings has emerged as a top contender to replace Leavitt after reportedly meeting with White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles.

summary: Donald Trump reportedly joked that his executive assistant, Natalie Harp, could potentially replace Karoline Leavitt as White House press secretary following Leavitt's unexpected departure. Trump also shared an AI-generated image of himself at the briefing room podium labeled "The Best Press Secretary." Meanwhile, political commentator Scott Jennings is considered a top contender for the role after meeting with White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles.
key_points: Donald Trump joked that executive assistant Natalie Harp could replace outgoing White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt.
Harp is known for providing Trump with printed news and social media posts, and has faced recent scrutiny over her role.
Trump posted an AI-generated image of himself at the press briefing room podium captioned "The Best Press Secretary."
Political commentator Scott Jennings emerged as a top contender to replace Leavitt after meeting with Susie Wiles.
White House officials expressed concern over Leavitt's departure due to the critical stability she and Wiles provided.

title: Israel re-establishes closed West Bank settlement, defying growing international protests
author: Lucy Williamson
content:
Watch: Israeli settlers return to settlement of Kadim
- Published
A new generation of Israeli settlers has returned to the settlement of Kadim, in the occupied West Bank, two decades after it was closed by a previous Israeli government.
Thirty "pioneer families" had arrived in the settlement on Thursday from Tel Aviv, according to the regional settlers' council, riding a wave of Jewish nationalism driven by Israel's current government.
They came in small groups, some under military escort, blue and white Israeli flags fluttering from their cars as they passed Palestinian villages and farmlands. Some dragged trailers loaded with bedding, furniture and building material.
Israel's government has overturned a 20-year ban on Jewish settlements around Jenin. Palestinian residents are watching the new push on settlement expansion here with fear.
All Israeli settlements and settler outposts are illegal under international law. Outposts are also illegal under Israeli law, though are often supported by state services and funding.
"21 years after the crime of expulsion from northern Samaria, we have completed the correction [â¦] and have returned to the settlement of Kadim," said Israel's far-right Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich at the opening ceremony, using the Biblical word for the northern West Bank.
Alongside him were Israel's Justice Minister, the Speaker of the Knesset, and Yossi Dagan, head of the regional settlers' council, who vowed that settlers would one day return to Gaza too.
Kadim, on a small hillside outside the Palestinian city of Jenin, was evacuated in 2005 by a previous Israeli government as part of a wider unilateral Disengagement Plan that also saw all Jewish settlers and soldiers pulled out of Gaza, and three other settlements in the northern West Bank dismantled.
At the time, the four settlements were considered too isolated and costly to protect, and of little strategic value.
![A group of men in shirts smiling and celebrating in the sunshine.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/813/cpsprodpb/b794/live/ca582060-9cdb-11f1-8c2c-67800657f112.jpg)
Senior Israeli politicians including Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich and Knesset Speaker Amir Ohana attended a national ceremony
In recent weeks, white trailer homes have appeared on the hilltop here again, in preparation for families to return.
Our request to speak to people at the opening ceremony was refused; we were told no media were allowed to enter the settlement today.
Driving along a dirt track on the hill behind it, we met a Palestinian vegetable farmer, living in the house he was born in 53 years ago.
He told me how, as a boy, he watched Kadim being built for the first time, then watched again as the settlers there were forced out by the government twenty years later.
"Back then, the settlers were living alongside us, and we coexisted peacefully. They lived their lives and we lived ours," he told me.
Now, watching them return, he's fearful.
"I'm afraid of the events spreading around us, and the bypass road [where] they demolished shops and businesses," he said.
"They drove my nephews away from their vegetables and citrus trees, telling them 'you have no place here, don't come back'".
He said his family fled here from Haifa during the 1948 Arab-Israeli War.
"There's no more displacement left in me," he said. "We're living with a sense of resignation. It's a life of fear."
After Kadim and the three other settlements here were evacuated in 2005, Israelis were banned from settling in this area. Israel's current government overturned that ban.
Kadim is the last of the settlements evacuated in 2005 to reopen. Ganim, Sanur and Homesh have already been formally opened, and families moved in.
But they are a drop in the ocean of the Israeli government's settlement project here. Since it took power in late 2022, it has approved more than 100 new settlements across the West Bank, including 19 in the northern West Bank.
![Two maps showing the significant growth in the numbers of Israeli settlements and settler outposts/farms across the occupied West Bank, excluding East Jerusalem, between December 2022 and July 2026](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1600/cpsprodpb/5455/live/89f9aeb0-8b12-11f1-a7ab-8b30adf0800a.png)
Hagit Ofran, director of the Settlement Watch programme at Peace Now, says the rapid construction in Jenin is part of a wider race by the Israeli government to expand settlements in the West Bank before Israeli elections are held in October.
One of those new settlements is Emek Dotan, to the west of Jenin, formally opened last Sunday and now home to almost two dozen Jewish families.
From the small hamlet of Palestinian houses next door to Emek Dotan, teacher Samer Jaber, has watched the settlement take shape: first the bulldozers, then the caravans lifted into place. The problems began even before most of the families moved in, he said.
"Groups come and stand opposite our houses, filming us," he told me.
"Yesterday they came and stood here, filming me and my children. Every time my wife stepped outside, they filmed her too. They try to enter our homes. And they go house by house, shining powerful floodlights directly through all the windows at two or three in the morning."
![A middle-aged Palestinian man with balding hair and a short beard.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/667/cpsprodpb/eaa6/live/79fc6bc0-9cdc-11f1-8c2c-67800657f112.jpg)
Problems began even before most of the families moved in, schoolteacher Samer Jaber told the BBC
Samer is partially blind and has a leg injury that makes moving difficult.
"Fear dominates everything. We are completely defenceless," he said. "All of them have weapons. I'm bringing concrete blocks to close off this side of the house because I'm afraid for my children."
Samer has watched settlements â and settler attacks â grow in other parts of the West Bank over the past few years, despite international pressure.
"Europe has no time for us, America is preoccupied with Iran, China has no interest," his analysis began. "Russia is busy with Ukraine, the United Nations is finished, and the Arab countries have their own internal problems."
"Democratic systems are over, they're finished," he concluded, anger and bitterness leaking out. "Civilisation, progress and modernity are lies."
Alongside the new settlements around Jenin, two new Israeli military bases are rapidly going up â construction vehicles churning up dust behind high concrete walls topped with watchtowers and barbed wire, Israeli flags flapping in the wind.
A military outpost is also being built on seized Palestinian land beside Jenin Refugee Camp â the first Israeli military base to be built on land under full Palestinian Authority control since the Oslo Accords were signed in 1993.
Israel's military evacuated thousands of residents from Jenin Refugee camp before occupying it in 2025.
The Israel Defence Forces confirmed that construction of the outpost in Jabriyat had been ordered "in accordance with operational needs".
The Palestinian Authority Governor for Jenin, Kamal Abu al-Rub, told me he was worried that Israel's seizure of land around the refugee camp signalled a plan to house settlers there, right in the heart of a Palestinian city, dividing it up like Hebron or Jerusalem.
He described the past two decades without settlers around Jenin as "bliss".
"Now, we live in the hell orchestrated by them and their assaults," he said. "It limits our movement. They cut off roads, bulldoze lands and cut down trees."
The speed of change here is breathtaking.
A few weeks ago, I sat drinking coffee in a cafÃ© on the road that runs from Kadim through the northern West Bank to Israel: now that cafÃ© â and dozens of Palestinian shops and businesses around it â are just piles of rubble along the road; demolished by the Israeli army.
The countdown to Israeli elections in October marked in the number of Palestinian buildings demolished, the number of new settler caravans.
summary: Israeli settlers have returned to the West Bank settlement of Kadim, overturning a 20-year ban implemented after the 2005 Disengagement Plan. Senior Israeli government officials attended the opening ceremony as part of a broader expansion of settlements and military infrastructure in the region. Palestinian residents near the settlements have reported fear, intimidation, movement restrictions, and the demolition of local businesses.
key_points: Thirty pioneer families arrived at the reopened Kadim settlement in the northern West Bank, two decades after it was evacuated.
The current Israeli government overturned a 20-year ban on settlements around Jenin, and all Israeli settlements are illegal under international law.
Senior Israeli politicians, including Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich and the Speaker of the Knesset, attended the official opening ceremony.
Local Palestinian residents expressed deep fear and described facing intimidation, property damage, movement restrictions, and business demolitions.

Construction of a new military outpost is underway on seized Palestinian land beside the Jenin Refugee Camp, marking the first such base on land under full Palestinian Authority control since the Oslo Accords.

title: Father leaves seven-year-old son alone on Mount Fuji for hours
author: Lily Shanagher
content:
Staff at a mountain hut alerted police to his presence after spotting him on his own at 7.30am local time (10.30pm UK time).
They invited the boy inside the hut and let him take shelter there while they waited for officers to arrive.
Officers contacted the father, who had reached the eighth station, and handed the boy over to him when he arrived.
It was estimated that the boy had been left for around three hours, Japan Today reported.
The police officer told AFP that officers gave the man a scolding for leaving the child behind.
“Even if it means having to give up on climbing the mountain together, leaving a child behind is unacceptable,” one told him, according to Japan Today.
‘Rash decision’
The father reportedly apologised to the police, admitting the act was careless. “I made a rash decision, and I deeply regret it,” he said.
The family had reportedly been following the Fujinomiya route up the mountain beginning at the fifth station, which is accessible via public transport.
It takes five hours to reach the peak from there and a further three hours to get down.
Every year, around 200,000 people climb the mountain, which is a popular landmark in Japan and located on the island of Honshu, south-west of Tokyo.
It is one of three traditional “Holy Mountains” along with Mount Tate and Mount Haku in Toyama Prefecture and Honshu respectively.
It is an active volcano and was granted World Heritage Status in 2013.
summary: A seven-year-old boy was left alone on Mount Fuji for approximately three hours after his father made the rash decision to climb ahead. Mountain hut staff found the boy and alerted police, who later scolded the father and reunited the child with him. The father apologized and admitted his actions were careless.
key_points: Mountain hut staff found the seven-year-old boy alone at 7:30 am local time and sheltered him until police arrived.
The father had climbed ahead to the eighth station, leaving the child behind for an estimated three hours.
Police strongly rebuked the father for abandoning the child, stating that leaving a child behind is unacceptable.
The father apologized to authorities, calling his choice a rash and careless decision that he deeply regrets.

title: Seventeen-year-old girl killed in sword attack at school in Sweden
author: Nadeem Badshah
content:
A 17-year-old girl has been killed after a teenager brandishing a sword attacked students at a school in Sweden, police have confirmed.
Three other people were wounded in the incident during classes in the central town of Fagersta on Friday afternoon, including two boys aged 12 and 17 who sustained minor injuries.
The third person, who was also under 18, was also left with minor injuries and has been discharged from hospital, Swedish news agency TT reported.
The parents of the 17-year-old girl told local newspaper Fagersta-Posten their daughter was killed in the attack.
An 18-year-old man has been arrested over the incident at Brinell high school.
![An armed police officer](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/f50063c87449022c4f687e262402af0331b48a48/0_0_5760_3840/master/5760.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Swedish police are investigating whether the suspect was involved in online communities promoting school violence, a police source said.
Detectives are investigating whether a TikTok account that posted a picture of a sword 20 minutes before the attack belonged to the person responsible, the source told Reuters.
The image appeared to have been taken in a restroom at the school, according to the Dagens Nyheter newspaper.
Before the image was taken down on Friday, the month-old account contained videos that referred to two episodes of mass violence in Sweden and to the far-right mass murderer Anders Behring Breivik, who killed 77 people in Norway in 2011.
One of the videos referenced a 2015 attack in which a masked swordsman killed a teaching assistant and two boys at a school in Trollhättan, western Sweden, before being shot dead by police.
“The investigators are looking into various online communities that may have egged on the suspect to carry out the attack,” the police source said.
Several party leaders cancelled planned speeches on Saturday, pausing campaigning ahead of Sweden’s 13 September general election.
![The Swedish prime minister, Ulf Kristersson, (L) and the Social Democratic party leader, Magdalena Andersson, visit the makeshift memorial.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/c9c84c5ab2c895fd73395d6453b81695bd85c3ba/0_0_8640_5760/master/8640.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
The prime minister, Ulf Kristersson, and opposition leader Magdalena Andersson travelled to Fagersta to offer condolences to the bereaved family and visit the injured.
Kristersson told reporters: “What should never happen has happened again. Our thoughts go first and foremost to the families who have been incredibly hard hit by this.”
Sweden’s worst mass shooting occurred in February 2025 at a school in the south-central city of Örebro, when a gunman killed 10 people before turning the weapon on himself.
On Saturday, the police clarified that the suspect in the Fagersta attack had not been shot, contrary to what they had said on Friday.
“Service weapons were used but the perpetrator has not been injured in connection with the arrest, and has not been in need of medical attention,” a police spokesperson told the Aftonbladet daily.
Prosecutors ordered the man’s detention on suspicion of murder and several counts of attempted murder.
summary: A 17-year-old girl was killed and three other minors were wounded in a sword attack at Brinell high school in Fagersta, Sweden. An 18-year-old man was arrested and detained on suspicion of murder and several counts of attempted murder. Police are investigating whether the suspect was linked to online communities that promote school violence.
key_points: A 17-year-old girl died following a sword attack at a school in Fagersta, Sweden.
Three other individuals under 18 sustained minor injuries during the incident.
An 18-year-old man was arrested and detained on suspicion of murder and attempted murder.
Police are investigating a TikTok account that posted a sword photo before the attack and referenced previous mass violence.

title: Magnitude 5.9 Earthquake Strikes Ibaraki Prefecture Outside of Tokyo
author: Weekender Editor
content:
A magnitude 5.9 earthquake struck Japan at around 2:00 a.m. Sunday morning. The quake registered a lower 5 on Japan’s seven-level seismic intensity scale in Ibaraki Prefecture.
According to the Japan Meteorological Agency (JMA), during a 5 tremor, “most people feel fear and feel the need to hold onto something. Dishes on shelves and books on bookshelves may fall.”
No Tsunami Warning Issued
The quake’s epicenter was located in southern Ibaraki Prefecture at a depth of 70 kilometers.
No tsunami warning has been issued.

Staying Informed on Earthquake Information

There are also a variety of helpful apps for earthquake safety. The Japan Tourism Agency has created the Safety Tips app for multilingual support that alerts users when there is an earthquake of magnitude four or higher or if there is a tsunami warning, as well as displaying evacuation tips. The NERV app shows real-time shaking throughout Japan, and estimated propagation in the affected areas.

title: Magnitude 5.9 earthquake rattles Tokyo and eastern Kanto region
author: Int-No Author
content:
Tokyo and the eastern Kanto region were shaken at 2 a.m. Sunday by a magnitude 5.9 earthquake centered in southern Ibaraki Prefecture at a depth of 70 kilometers. There was no threat of a tsunami.
Shaking was recorded at an intensity of lower 5 on Japan’s seven-point shindo seismic scale in Tokyo’s Adachi Ward as well as in Ibaraki, Saitama and Chiba prefectures. Level 4 shaking was recorded in other areas of Tokyo as well as Tochigi, Gunma and Kanagawa prefectures.
Lower 5 can cause objects to fall off shelves and prompt people to grab onto things due to severe shaking, according to the Meteorological Agency.
Shaking, lasting up to a minute in some areas, was felt shortly after earthquake early warning alarms sounded on mobile phones.
According to NHK, Level 2 long-period ground motion was observed in the city of Kawaguchi in Saitama Prefecture, the city of Urayasu in Chiba Prefecture, as well as in Tokyo’s Koto and Edogawa wards. Long-period ground motion refers to slow, prolonged shaking that can cause high-rise buildings to sway significantly. At Level 2, people may have difficulty standing, and furniture or other objects may move or fall.
Authorities in the affected areas were working to confirm whether the quake had caused injuries or damage, with the city of Kawasaki reporting two injuries as of 3 a.m., according to NHK.
A water pipe had ruptured in the Kiyosumi area of Tokyo’s Koto Ward, but it is not yet known if this was caused by the earthquake, news reports said.
JR East was in the process of checking whether the quake had caused any damage and will decide whether first trains can operate as usual by 4:30 a.m., NHK reported.
In the village of Tokai in Ibaraki Prefecture, home to Japan Atomic Power Company’s Tokai and Tokai No. 2 nuclear power plants, shaking was recorded at an intensity of 3 on the shindo scale. The Japan Atomic Power Company said no abnormalities had been found at the Tokai No. 2 plant following the earthquake, and that checks were ongoing at its Tokai nuclear plant. The Tokai plant is currently being decommissioned, while the Tokai No. 2 plant has been offline for an extended period.
Within an hour of the quake, Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi wrote on X that efforts to confirm the extent of earthquake impacts were ongoing and that a liaison office had been established following the quake at the Prime Minister’s Office Crisis Management Center. She added that she had issued instructions to establish the extent of any damage and to provide timely and accurate information to the public.
“To those in the areas where the shaking was strong, I ask that you continue to remain vigilant for the possibility of another earthquake of similar magnitude,” the prime minister said.
More information:
summary: A magnitude 5.9 earthquake struck the eastern Kanto region and Tokyo at 2 a.m. Sunday, causing lower 5 intensity shaking in parts of Tokyo, Ibaraki, Saitama, and Chiba prefectures. No tsunami threat was issued, and authorities began checking for injuries and damage while monitoring infrastructure like railways and nuclear facilities. Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi urged residents in strongly shaken areas to remain vigilant for potential aftershocks.
key_points: The earthquake was centered in southern Ibaraki Prefecture at a depth of 70 kilometers with no tsunami threat.
Lower 5 seismic intensity was recorded in Tokyo's Adachi Ward as well as Ibaraki, Saitama, and Chiba prefectures.
Kawasaki reported two injuries, and authorities were working to confirm other potential damage.
No abnormalities were initially found at the Tokai No. 2 nuclear power plant.
Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi established a liaison office and urged the public to stay vigilant for similar aftershocks.

title: Man leaves young son on Mount Fuji before ascending Japan’s highest peak
author: Donna Ferguson
content:
A man who abandoned his seven-year-old son on Mount Fuji in Japan after the boy complained of feeling tired while on a family hike has been reprimanded by local police.
A worker on Japan’s highest mountain discovered the child sitting alone on a bench near the sixth station of the Fujinomiya trail at an altitude of more than 2,000 metres (6,500 feet) on Thursday.
After inviting the boy to take shelter at the station, the worker called the police, who took the child into protective custody.
It emerged that he had told his father he was too tired to continue while they were hiking up the trail in the early hours of the morning.
The man, who was from Japan’s fourth-largest city, Nagoya, gave his son some snacks and a soft drink.
He then told him to wait for him before continuing his five-hour ascent to the summit with the child’s older brother, who had already gone on ahead. It would have taken him about eight hours to return, according to local reports.
By the time police officers managed to contact the boy’s father, he had ascended to the eighth station, a three-hour hike from where he had left his son.
They told him to turn back, and after reuniting him with his son reprimanded him for leaving the child alone on an active volcano.
“Even if it means having to give up on climbing the mountain together, leaving a child behind is unacceptable,” officers said, according to Japan Today.
Weather on the mountain, which has its own microclimate, is unpredictable and can change rapidly. Hypothermia poses a serious risk for hikers even in the summer.
The father is said to have apologised to the police, saying: “I made a rash decision, and I deeply regret it.”
Local police are urging hikers to consider the abilities and stamina of everyone in their group when planning an ascent on Mount Fuji, and to adjust their pace accordingly.
summary: A man in Japan was reprimanded by police after abandoning his seven-year-old son on Mount Fuji because the boy was too tired to continue the hike. A mountain worker discovered the child alone on a bench at an altitude of over 2,000 meters and notified the authorities, who placed the boy in protective custody. Police contacted the father higher up the trail, ordered him to turn back, and reunited the family while criticizing his rash decision.
key_points: A seven-year-old boy was left alone on Mount Fuji by his father after feeling too tired to hike.
A mountain worker found the child at the sixth station and called the police for protective custody.
The father continued his ascent to the summit with his older son before police contacted him and ordered him to turn back.
Local police severely reprimanded the father for abandoning his child on an active volcano where weather and hypothermia are serious risks.
The father apologized and expressed deep regret for his rash decision.

title: Carney calls Trump's fresh tariffs a 'miscalculation' after trade talks collapse
author: Nadine Yousif
content:
![Mark Carney gestures as he talks in front of two Canadian flags](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1024/cpsprodpb/ae91/live/dc71e910-9e49-11f1-8871-ff7211da55c9.jpg)
- Published
Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney has said a fresh wave of US tariffs on Canada is a "miscalculation" designed to "hurt and divide us", after trade talks broke down late on Friday.
Carney said he walked away from a deal because he was not prepared to "compromise Canada's sovereignty", adding he felt the country was being "attacked" by the US.
"They asked too much and they offered too little," Carney said in a speech to Canadians on Saturday morning.
The prime minister said that Canada will match US tariffs "dollar-for-dollar" from 8 September, including levies on steel, dairy, appliances and electronics. Donald Trump has yet to comment.
Both countries were optimistic of a deal earlier in the week, but talks collapsed on Friday night after both sides accused the other of making last-minute changes.
Now that talks have broken down, Canada has been hit with new 50% US tariffs on a range of Canadian goods, in addition to existing US tariffs on Canadian steel, aluminium, automobiles and lumber.
The prime minister said Canada was retaliating "reluctantly" to protect its interests. Details of the counter-measures will be released in the coming days, he said.
Carney's speech on Saturday was his first address to Canadians after he announced late on Friday night that a deal would not be reached, accusing the Americans of making "last-minute changes" that were "unfair" and "uneconomic".
US negotiators, meanwhile, accused Canada of making "new demands and walk backs" on terms which had been agreed earlier in the week.
On Saturday, US trade representative Jamieson Greer told Fox News there were no plans to resume talks.
He added that the US had been prepared to cut some of its tariffs on Canada as part of the deal that fell apart.
"They've always had the best deal, and they still would have an even better deal, but they didn't want that," said Greer.
Carney, however, said the US presented "unacceptable" terms that were too restrictive, including curbing Canada's ability to strike new trade deals with other countries.
The prime minister also rejected the assertion that Canada had made last-minute requests: "We clarified what was on offer and were continually disappointed by the answers."
The collapse comes after more than a year of on-again, off-again trade talks, which intensified in recent weeks after a US-imposed deadline to strike a deal or face further tariffs.
The two countries were also engaged in a mandatory review of an existing North American free trade agreement, known as USMCA, with Mexico.
The pact was signed by Trump during his first term to replace the 1994 North American Free Trade Agreement. It underpins $1.6tn (Â£1.2tn) in annual trilateral trade across Canada, the US and Mexico.
Earlier this summer, Canada and Mexico had formally requested for USMCA to be renewed for another 16 years. The US, however, declined to renew it in its current form.
Asked how Friday's trade talk collapse would impact the North American free trade pact, Carney said it was "certainly not good news".
Tariffs - a tax placed on imports from other countries - have been a key component of Trump's trade policy, with the US president arguing they will boost American manufacturing and create jobs at home.
Critics, however, say tariffs have raised prices for American consumers and have disrupted and damaged the global economy.

Canada announced it will match US tariffs dollar-for-dollar starting September 8, following disputes over last-minute changes and sovereignty. US officials stated there are currently no plans to resume negotiations.
key_points: Trade talks between the US and Canada collapsed late Friday after both sides blamed each other for last-minute changes.
Prime Minister Mark Carney stated he walked away to protect Canada's sovereignty and announced dollar-for-dollar retaliatory tariffs beginning September 8.
The US imposed new 50% tariffs on a range of Canadian goods following the breakdown of talks.
US trade representative Jamieson Greer stated there are no plans to resume negotiations.
The collapse impacts the ongoing review of the USMCA trade agreement after the US declined to renew it in its current form.

title: Carney faces crucial test after calling Trump's bluff
author: Jessica Murphy
content:
![Mark Carney stands in profile, facing to the left, against a clear light blue sky. He wears a dark blue suit and tie.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/999/cpsprodpb/7965/live/5fe534d0-9e38-11f1-aed2-8d6da8d75094.jpg)
- Published
The United States and Canada have entered into uncharted territory.
The longtime allies and economic partners, who have enjoyed free trade for decades, are now in an escalating trade war with no clear off ramp.
And for Prime Minister Mark Carney, the late night decision to suspend talks with President Donald Trump and to retaliate instead of agreeing to a deal that seemed in reach, will be a significant political test.
He is one of the first world leaders to walk away from the negotiating table with the White House - and the outcome will be closely watched.
Both sides have have blamed last-minute changes for torpedoing the tentative deal.
Carney's decision will also challenge the appetite among Canadians to accept some economic pain as Ottawa pushes for more US concessions.
After rejecting Trump's high pressure tactics, and in choosing to hit back against the latest duties, Carney will need to convince Canadians that the economic pain is worth the cost of standing up to the Trump administration in search of a better agreement in the long run.
There is no doubt this will cause pain on both sides of the border, with business facing more pressure from US duties and Canadian counter-tariffs.
Canada sends about 70% of its exports to the US, and the country is the top trading partner for a number of US states, with Michigan, Kentucky, Indiana and Ohio among the most exposed.
Carney came to power with a call for "elbows up" - an ice-hockey term for an aggressive approach - vowing to fight for Canada in the face of a Trump administration keen to exert economic pressure for its America First agenda.
Many Canadians have told pollsters that they are willing to fight.
A recent survey by Abacus Data suggested that around 36% of Canadians would support retaliating to US tariffs, while a Leger poll indicated that 56% of Canadians want the federal government to take a hard line and make no more concessions.
Canadians frustrated with the US tariffs have already chosen to avoid travelling there. The boycott has meant a loss of about C$3.3bn ($2.35bn; Â£1.75bn) in travel revenue for the US last year.
A decision by most provinces to remove US alcohol from store shelves has hammered that sector.
Based on US government trade data, US wine exports to Canada fell 78% year over year, a $357m loss in export value. The US distillers association reported similar numbers - saying provincial bans have caused exports of American spirits to drop by more than 70%.
The ban quickly became a point of frustration for the Trump administration.
Canadaâs prime minister will also need to convince the provinces who have been less affected by the US trade dispute so far that walking away is a risk worth taking.
He will be meeting them on Saturday to brief them on the current state of affairs.
What went wrong?
For a week, it seemed that a deal between Washington and Ottawa was in reach.
It's still unclear exactly how the talks fell apart in the final hours.
Carney said that late US proposed terms "were unfair, uneconomic, and called into question the reliability of any deal".
US trade representative Jamieson Greer pointed to "new demands and walk backs of other commitments by Canada".
In a statement on Friday, the Distilled Spirits Council of the United States suggested "Canadian provinces' continued refusal to return US spirits products to store shelves has led to this outcome".
Both Ontario and Quebec had yet to say whether they were on board with a reversal on the US booze boycott.
There were also reports by Canadian media, external that US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, was unhappy with the deal.
And as details on an interim trade agreement with the US trickled out over last week, some provincial leaders, industry groups and political opponents raised concerns that the prime minister had not delivered on the fight he promised.
Conservative opposition leader Pierre Poilievre said that any agreement that included "one-sided" tariffs on Canadian industry would be "a bad deal".
On Saturday, he backed Carney's decision to walk away for now, saying: "Canada cannot accept one-sided tariffs that will deindustrialise our country."
Doug Ford, the premier of Ontario and usually one of the most vocal Canadian politicians on US tariffs, had been silent on the tentative deal.
But in a letter sent to Carney this week, and released later by his office, Ford raised concerns that an agreement under pressure from the US would âembolden the United States to seek concession after concession".
The province, which has a large manufacturing and vehicle sector, has been among the hardest hit regions in this trade dispute.
After negotiations broke down, Ford said "the prime minister has my full support for a strong response - tariff for tariff, dollar for dollar".
Now Carney - and Canada - must wait to see how Trump responds.
summary: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney faces a major political test after suspending trade talks with President Donald Trump and opting to retaliate against US duties instead of accepting a tentative deal. Both sides blamed last-minute changes for collapsing the negotiations, which now plunges the longtime economic partners into an escalating trade war. Carney must convince Canadians and provincial leaders that enduring near-term economic pain is worth the cost of standing up to the Trump administration for a better long-term agreement.
key_points: Prime Minister Mark Carney suspended trade talks with President Donald Trump and chose to retaliate against US duties rather than accept a tentative agreement.
Both the US and Canada blamed last-minute changes and new demands for torpedoing the deal in its final hours.
Carney must convince Canadians and less-affected provinces that enduring short-term economic pain is worthwhile to secure a better long-term trade agreement.
Canadian retaliatory measures, including provincial boycotts of US alcohol, have already caused significant financial losses for American exporters.
Opposition figures, including Conservative leader Pierre Poilievre and Ontario Premier Doug Ford, expressed support for Carney's decision to walk away from a one-sided deal.

title: Russian strikes kill 6 people in Ukraine, day after shopping complex attack
author: Al Jazeera staff; AP; Reuters
content:
![This handout photograph taken and released by the Dnipropetrovsk Regional Military Administration on August 21, 2026 shows firefighters taking part in operations against a fire at the site of a shopping mall damaged following a Russian strike in Kryvyi Rih amid the Russian invasion of Ukraine.](https://www.aljazeera.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/afp_6a895a729448-1787386482.jpg?resize=770%2C513&quality=80)
Russian aerial strikes on Ukraine have killed at least six people and injured 26 others, while a Ukrainian drone attack hit a house in southern Russia, killing two children and injuring their parents, officials on both sides said.
Kyiv’s Mayor Vitali Klitschko confirmed on Saturday morning that one person was killed in a warehouse fire in the Darnytskyi district following an overnight Russian ballistic missile attack.

- list 4 of 4Several killed in Russia’s ‘double-tap’ drone strike on Ukraine mall
In the Kherson region, three others were killed and 13 wounded after Russian strikes damaged homes and apartment buildings, the regional military administration reported.
In Donetsk region, Russian attacks left one person dead and seven wounded, including five in the front-line city of Kramatorsk, according to regional governor Vadym Filashkin, local media reported. In the Sumy region, a drone strike on a house killed one man, while six others were hurt in separate drone attacks across the region, regional officials said, according to reports.
In the city of Kherson itself, a drone strike set a shopping centre ablaze, though no casualties were reported, reports said.
On the other side, in Russia’s southern Krasnodar region, authorities said two children were killed and two adults wounded in a Ukrainian drone strike.
The latest attacks coincided with ongoing rescue operations in Kryvyi Rih, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s hometown, where emergency workers searched the charred wreckage of the Sunny Gallery shopping complex following Friday afternoon’s assault.
Oleksandr Vilkul, head of the Kryvyi Rih Defense Council, said Russian forces targeted the city’s largest shopping centre with jet-powered Shahed drones.
A second wave hit roughly 30 minutes after the first on Friday, allegedly targeting emergency crews responding to the scene.
Dnipropetrovsk regional governor Oleksandr Hanzha confirmed in an update on Saturday morning that the death toll in Kryvyi Rih had risen to 16, with more than 130 wounded, including 22 children.
Zelenskyy called Friday’s attack “absolutely cynical and despicable” and an “act of barbarism”, promising a swift response. “Attacks like these are nothing less than terrorist acts,” he posted on Telegram.
Al Jazeera’s Audrey MacAlpine, reporting from Kyiv, said Friday’s attack began “at 4:30 in the afternoon when the mall is typically crowded,” with a second wave following “just 30 minutes later, with rescue workers from nearby regions called in to help”.
“The attacks come as civilian casualties in the war continue to mount, with July marking one of the deadliest months for civilians on both sides since the full-scale war began. And they are another example of how attacks far beyond the front lines are taking their toll on ordinary people,” she said.
summary: Recent Russian aerial strikes across multiple regions in Ukraine have killed at least six people and injured 26 others. Meanwhile, a Ukrainian drone attack in southern Russia resulted in the deaths of two children and injuries to their parents. These incidents follow a deadly double-tap drone strike on a shopping complex in Kryvyi Rih that left 16 dead and over 130 wounded.
key_points: Russian strikes across Ukraine killed six people and injured 26.
A Ukrainian drone attack in Russia's Krasnodar region killed two children and injured their parents.
The death toll from the Kryvyi Rih shopping center strike rose to 16, with over 130 wounded.
The Kryvyi Rih assault involved a double-tap drone strike that reportedly targeted emergency crews.

title: It’s a miracle: Natalie Harp has turned Republicans into feminists | Arwa Mahdawi
author: Arwa Mahdawi
content:
Jon Ossoff is quite the miracle worker. Perhaps the Democratic senator can’t turn water into wine, but he has managed to turn whining conservatives into impassioned feminists.
During a rally last Sunday, the Georgia senator delivered a takedown of Donald Trump, which included a reference to his aide Natalie Harp. “He doesn’t want to do the job,” Ossoff said of the president. “He wants to build his ballroom and travel with Natalie on their apparently defenseless flying palace gifted by the Emir of Qatar.”
Those three words – travel with Natalie – were deliberately loaded. Harp was in the spotlight at the time because of the decoy plane story. The 35-year-old was one of a handful of people Trump had taken onto a different plane via a catering truck when he was worried about a potential assassination attack targeting Air Force One. Intrigue as to the exact nature of the relationship between Harp and Trump was heightened by the fact that Melania Trump, the president’s third wife, hadn’t been seen in public for weeks at the time. (Funnily enough, she magically reappeared on Thursday, a few days after Ossoff’s comments, for a press conference where she lovingly held hands with Trump. Very cute.)
Ossoff’s remarks about “Natalie” might have been something of a cheap shot, but it’s hilarious to watch the right discover misogyny and decry the remarks as sexist. Suddenly, everyone from Fox News to prominent conservatives are very worried about a professional woman not being taken seriously.
The former House speaker Newt Gingrich, for example, said on Twitter/X that Ossoff owes Harp an apology. “If a conservative Republican had attacked a liberal Democrat working professional woman the way Ossoff smeared Natalie Harp there would be cries to kick them off the ticket and reject this kind of misogynistic language diminishing and smearing someone who is simply doing their job.”
The conservative commentator Scott Jennings, who is rumoured to be a potential replacement for Karoline Leavitt as White House press secretary, was also appalled. “[Ossoff] unleashed a comment so vile against a young Republican woman working in politics that every woman in this country, no matter your ideology, ought to listen carefully and never forget it,” Jennings said on his podcast.
Meghan McCain also clutched her pearls at the coverage Ossoff’s comments sparked. “The egregious sexist attacks on Natalie Harp are absolutely insane – and they’re coming from prestigious journalists,” she wrote on X. “What is wrong with everyone?! Every president has close aides and sometimes they are females. Like what year is this?!”
It’s 2026, Meghan. And in the year 2026 I think the masses have generally understood that simply criticizing a woman is not in itself misogynistic. I’m not saying there hasn’t been any misogyny in the Harp coverage, but the main reason there has been so much attention on the story is because the White House has had a completely unhinged response to Ossoff’s comments and kept it in the news. More importantly, the reason so many people aren’t taking the Trump aide seriously isn’t because she’s a woman; it’s because she’s not a serious person.
And I’m being diplomatic with that choice of language. After all, we’re talking about someone whose nickname is “the human printer” because, while working on Trump’s re-election campaign, she reportedly ran around after him with a portable printer, handing him hard copies of flattering coverage. You could write that off as a canny career move from someone who understands flattery gets you everywhere with Trump, but that’s also one of the least weird things Harp has done. Per a CNN report, which has pictures of the incident, back in 2023, Harp jumped in the trunk of an SUV because she wanted to be close to Trump and there was no room in his motorcade. Once Trump won re-election and Harp joined him in the White House, she apparently worked for a year without security clearance. According to reporting by MS NOW, she declined to complete the clearance process for unknown reasons.
And then there are the “adoring letters” Harp sent Trump, first mentioned in the book Regime Change, by the New York Times reporters Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan. Two were later published in the Daily Beast. “You are all that matters to me,” she wrote in one letter. Other memorable lines included “I want to bring you joy, to feel like we can get through a day without ever having to talk ‘work’”; she also called Trump her “Guardian and Protector in this Life”.
To state the obvious: these are deeply weird things to say to your boss. (It’s also weird that Harp shares Trump’s unconventional approach to capitalization.) I should note that Harp, who says she is a cancer survivor, seems to believe that Trump saved her life by signing legislation that gave her access to experimental bone cancer treatment when she was younger. While that might make her obsession with Trump more understandable, it does not make her general conduct any more professional. So spare me all the lectures from the right about sexism, please. If you’re worried about how women in politics are treated, you should probably focus your attention on the adjudicated sexual abuser who is president.
Donald Trump attacks another female journalist
Trump can’t seem to stand it when a woman doesn’t fawn over him and has a history of attacking female journalists. The latest object of his ire is the CNN reporter Kristen Holmes, who asked the president about Ossoff’s comments regarding Natalie Harp. Trump called Holmes a “loud boisterous person” and instructed her to be “quiet”. Meanwhile, the White House’s social media account posted about Holmes multiple times. In one post they wrote: “Someday, your children will come across your disgusting and inhumane question. They will be sickened and embarrassed to have a parent be so callous and vindictive.”
New York gives parents a ‘night out’
New York mayor Zohran Mamdani hosted the city’s first Parents’ Night Out. The city provided free childcare for nearly 300 kids so parents could have a little time off. This is what “family values” and being pro-life actually look like: supporting parents, not forcing women to give birth.

title: Iran says new US sanctions violate sovereignty of other states
author: Al Jazeera Staff
content:
![A woman walks next to an anti-Trump billboard.](https://www.aljazeera.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/epa_6a89588c8227-1787385996.jpg?resize=770%2C513&quality=80)
Iran has decried impending United States sanctions as a “complete erosion of sovereignty” following US President Donald Trump’s threat to punish any country doing business with Tehran.
In a post on X on Saturday, Iran’s Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said the US announcement was “an assertion of extraterritorial sovereignty” against the United Nations’ member states.

No state can compel foreign banks, enterprises or airports to renounce commerce with Iran, he said.
“The end result would be the complete erosion of sovereignty as the foundational basis of the UN-based inter-State system, and a recipe for an abysmal return to full-scale classic colonialism,” Baghaei said.
Trump announced on Wednesday the “most crushing economic operation” yet against Iran and said any country whose institutions interface with Tehran would face “tremendous economic consequences”.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent doubled down on the president’s words on Thursday, saying the new sanctions regime would “collapse” Iran and that other countries are “either with us or against us”.
Iranian state media was quick to point out that Tehran has faced US sanctions for decades. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said the new measures were “bound to fail”.
“We have seen this movie before,” Araghchi wrote on X, alongside a screenshot of a tweet from former President Barack Obama referencing earlier sanctions in 2012. “Same bull. Different bullies.”
The latest rhetorical back-and-forth comes as peace talks with Tehran have sputtered out. The US Navy has maintained its blockade against Iran’s ports, while oil shipment traffic through the Strait of Hormuz has virtually ceased.
Trump told reporters Friday that his government is “seeing what happens” in the conflict.
“They would love to make a deal, but they’re not ready to make the right deal in my opinion,” the president said.
While the US has blockaded Iranian vessels in their ports, the Strait of Hormuz remained bottled up with thousands of seafarers stranded on hundreds of vessels.
Only four commodity ships sailed along the strait on Thursday, none of them large crude carriers or liquefied natural gas tankers, ship-tracking data showed.
However, Iran has granted permission for several Iraqi oil tankers to pass through the strait following repeated requests from Baghdad, Iran’s state news agency IRNA reported on Saturday.
IRNA said obtaining special permission for Iraqi tankers was one of Baghdad’s main requests during Iranian parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf’s visit to Iraq.
summary: Iran has condemned impending US sanctions and threats of punishment for countries doing business with Tehran as an assertion of extraterritorial sovereignty that violates international norms. US President Donald Trump announced the new economic measures, while Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent stated that the sanctions aim to collapse Iran and force other nations to choose a side. Amid stalled peace talks and a US naval blockade that has virtually halted oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz, Iranian officials dismissed the measures as bound to fail.
key_points: Iran's Foreign Ministry stated that new US sanctions violate the sovereignty of UN member states and resemble classic colonialism.
US President Donald Trump announced severe economic penalties for any country doing business with Tehran.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent asserted that the new sanctions regime would collapse Iran and demanded other nations align with the US.
A US naval blockade has effectively stopped oil traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, though Iran permitted a few Iraqi oil tankers to pass.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi dismissed the new measures, stating that decades of prior US sanctions have failed.

title: Lindsay Clancy suffering 'command hallucination' when she killed children, court hears
author: Ana Faguy
content:
![Lindsay Clancy sits and looks off to the side while wearing a peach coloured shirt](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1024/cpsprodpb/9ec0/live/e9fd5290-9d9f-11f1-b160-9b29341ab62f.jpg)
- Published
Warning: This story contains distressing details and discussion of attempted suicide
Lindsay Clancy, the Massachusetts mum who has been charged with murdering her three children, was suffering from a "command hallucination" at the time, a forensic psychiatrist has told the jury in her trial.
The defence, which rested its case on Friday, does not dispute that Clancy carried out the killings but say she has pleaded not guilty to murder charges because she was experiencing postpartum psychosis.
Forensic psychiatrist Phillip Resnick, the defence's final witness, testified about the effects of postpartum psychosis.
Prosecutors, meanwhile, alleged she made a calculated decision to intentionally kill her children - Cora, five, Dawson, three, and Callan, who was eight months.
"My opinion is that Ms Clancy was, due to her mental disease, unable to conform her conduct to the requirements of the law on the day that she took the lives of her children," Resnick told jurors. "It was a matter where she was just following the command rather than being able to make any decision to do it or not."
The forensic psychiatrist said that in his opinion on the day Clancy killed her children she experienced "not only a command hallucination" but also "a delusion of influence".
Resnick evaluated Clancy after the killings and reviewed her medical records.
Watch: What is postpartum psychosis and why is it central in the Lindsay Clancy trial?
Clancy lacked control and was likely unable to tell the difference between right and wrong on that January 2023 day, he told the jury on Friday.
"In her mind, she believed that she would be doing her children a favour by having them go to heaven with her rather than remain on earth without her doing the mothering," Resnick testified.
The case is expected to go to the jury early next week following nearly a month of witness testimony.
Earlier this week, Clancy's mother and former mother-in-law testified about how Clancy's mental health deteriorated after the birth of her youngest son.
"She was begging for help," Clancy's former mother-in-law, Susan Clancy, said of a woman she described as a "very nurturing, very loving" mother.
Clancy has been charged with three counts of first-degree murder.
Prosecutors have said that in January 2023, Clancy intentionally strangled the three children with fitness bands in their Massachusetts home before jumping out of a second-floor window. Clancy, now 36, was paralysed by the jump and has attended the trial in a wheelchair.
The defence have said Clancy experienced hallucinations and delusions after giving birth to Callan and she was undergoing medical treatment for psychiatric problems. She checked herself into a psychiatric hospital for a few days just before the deaths.
The UK's National Health Service (NHS) defines postpartum psychosis as a rare serious mental health illness that can affect someone soon after having a baby.
"Postpartum psychosis is very different from the 'baby blues'," the NHS adds. "It's a serious mental illness and should be treated as a medical emergency."
If you are suffering distress or despair and need support, you could speak to a health professional, or an organisation that offers support. Details of help available in many countries can be found at Befrienders Worldwide. www.befrienders.org.
In the UK a list of organisations that can help is available at bbc.co.uk/actionline.
summary: During her trial for the murder of her three children in January 2023, a forensic psychiatrist testified that Lindsay Clancy was suffering from a command hallucination and postpartum psychosis. While the defence argues she was unable to control her actions or tell right from wrong due to mental disease, prosecutors allege she made a calculated decision to kill the children. The case is expected to go to the jury following nearly a month of testimony.
key_points: Lindsay Clancy has pleaded not guilty to murder charges regarding the deaths of her three children.
A forensic psychiatrist testified that Clancy experienced a command hallucination and postpartum psychosis during the incident.
Prosecutors argue that Clancy made a calculated decision to intentionally kill her children.
Clancy was paralysed after jumping from a second-floor window following the killings.
Family members previously testified that Clancy's mental health had severely deteriorated after the birth of her youngest son.
